q: If I _______ you, I would accept that assignment.
e: Second conditional: 'If I were you' (subjunctive 'were' for all persons).

q: If it rains tomorrow, we _______ the field exercise.
e: First conditional: if + present, will + base verb.

q: If they had left earlier, they _______ the convoy.
e: Third conditional: if + past perfect, would have + past participle.

q: Unless you study, you _______ the ECL.
e: Unless = if not; first conditional takes 'will/won't'.

q: If water reaches 100°C, it _______.
e: Zero conditional (general truth): if + present, present.

q: I would have called you if I _______ your number.
e: Third conditional: if + past perfect (had + past participle). The past participle of *have* is *had*: if I had had your number.

q: _______ I in charge, I would change the schedule.
e: Formal inversion: 'Were I...' = 'If I were...'.

q: If the colonel _______ here now, he would order a withdrawal.
e: Second conditional (unreal present): 'were'.

q: You _______ salute a superior officer. It is mandatory.
e: 'Must' expresses obligation.

q: Soldiers _______ wear civilian clothes on duty. It is forbidden.
e: 'Must not' = prohibition. 'Don't have to' = no obligation.

q: You _______ attend the ceremony; it is optional.
e: Absence of obligation = 'don't have to'.

q: He isn't answering his phone. He _______ be in a briefing.
e: 'Might' = possibility (perhaps he is).

q: That _______ be Commander Whitfield — he was deployed overseas last week.
e: 'Can't be' = logical impossibility in the present.

q: You _______ seen a doctor earlier. Now the infection is worse.
e: 'Should have + past participle' = past advice not followed (regret/reproach).

q: The lights are on in the command post; someone _______ be inside.
e: 'Must be' = logical deduction (certainty).

q: _______ you help me carry this equipment, please?
e: 'Could you...?' = polite request.

q: The orders _______ by the major yesterday.
e: Passive, past simple: were + past participle.

q: English _______ at every major staff college in the world.
e: Passive, present simple: is + past participle.

q: The bridge _______ by army engineers next month.
e: Passive, future: will be + past participle.

q: The suspect _______ by the military police right now.
e: Passive, present continuous: is being + past participle.

q: The report _______ yet.
e: Passive, present perfect: hasn't been + past participle.

q: My wallet _______! Call the security office.
e: Passive, present perfect: has been stolen.

q: The new recruits _______ basic first aid last week.
e: Passive: the recruits receive the action, so were taught.

q: The success of the mission depends _______ accurate intelligence.
e: Depend *on* something.

q: She is married _______ a naval officer.
e: Married *to* someone.

q: We arrived _______ the airport at noon.
e: Arrive *at* a place (airport, station); arrive *in* a city/country.

q: I have been waiting _______ two hours.
e: 'For' + duration; 'since' + starting point.

q: He has served on this base _______ 2019.
e: 'Since' + starting point in time.

q: The staff meeting is _______ Monday morning.
e: *On* + days and dates; *in* + months/years; *at* + clock times.

q: He is very good _______ solving logistical problems.
e: Good *at* something.

q: _______ Pacific is the largest ocean in the world.
e: Use *the* with oceans, seas and rivers: the Pacific, the Atlantic, the Mediterranean, the Nile.

q: She is _______ honest and reliable officer.
e: 'Honest' starts with a vowel *sound* → an.

q: _______ Nile flows through Egypt.
e: *The* + rivers, seas, oceans (the Nile, the Atlantic).

q: I go to _______ work by car every day.
e: No article in fixed expressions: go to work / go to bed.

q: He became _______ officer in 2010.
e: Professions take a/an; 'officer' begins with a vowel sound → an.

q: I enjoy _______ in the ocean early in the morning.
e: Enjoy + gerund (-ing).

q: She decided _______ the naval academy.
e: Decide + to + infinitive.

q: He avoided _______ the journalist's question.
e: Avoid + gerund.

q: They agreed _______ the new operational plan.
e: Agree + to + infinitive.

q: I look forward to _______ from you soon.
e: 'Look forward to' + gerund ('to' is a preposition here).

q: Would you mind _______ the window?
e: Mind + gerund.

q: He stopped _______ two years ago, on the doctor's advice.
e: Stop + gerund = quit the habit. Stop + to-infinitive = pause in order to do it.

q: He can swim across the bay, _______?
e: Modal repeats in the tag: can → can't he.

q: Nobody was hurt in the accident, _______?
e: 'Nobody' → tag with 'they' and positive verb: were they?

q: This exam was _______ than the last one.
e: Short adjective → -er + than.

q: It is the _______ decision he has ever made.
e: Irregular superlative: bad → worse → the worst.

q: The more you train, the _______ you become.
e: Parallel comparative: 'The more..., the stronger...'.

q: She speaks English much _______ than her brother.
e: Irregular comparative of 'well': better.

q: This is by far _______ route to the base.
e: Superlative with 'the': the shortest.

q: He is not as tall _______ his father.
e: Equality structure: as + adjective + as.

q: I wish I _______ taller.
e: Wish + past subjunctive for present unreal situations.

q: If only I _______ harder for the ECL last year.
e: Regret about the past: if only + past perfect.

q: He _______ smoke, but he quit two years ago.
e: 'Used to + base verb' = past habit that has stopped.

q: I'm not used to _______ up so early.
e: 'Be used to' + gerund = be accustomed to.

q: I had my dress uniform _______ before the parade.
e: Causative: have + object + past participle (someone did it for me).

q: The drill instructor made the recruits _______ ten miles.
e: Make + object + base verb (no 'to').

q: She got her car _______ at the garage on base.
e: Get + object + past participle (causative).

q: The instructor let us _______ early on Friday.
e: Let + object + base verb (no 'to').

q: It's high time we _______ for the harbor.
e: 'It's high time' + past tense (subjunctive meaning).

q: I'd rather you _______ mention this to anyone.
e: 'Would rather + subject' + past tense: I'd rather you didn't.

q: The commander insisted that every soldier _______ present at 0600.
e: American subjunctive after insist/demand/require: that + base verb (be).

q: It is essential that she _______ on time for the board.
e: Subjunctive after 'it is essential/important that': base verb.

q: There isn't _______ time left before the deadline.
e: Much + uncountable (time); many + countable.

q: _______ soldiers volunteered for the night mission.
e: Several + plural countable noun.

q: He has very _______ friends in this garrison town.
e: Few + countable plural (= almost none).

q: Could I have _______ water, please?
e: 'Some' in polite requests and offers.

q: There are too _______ mistakes in this report.
e: Many + countable plural (mistakes).

q: The new radar ______ three false alarms since the technicians updated its software on Monday.
e: 'Since' + a past point (Monday) needs the present perfect in the main clause: has triggered.

q: I ______ on this report since 0700, and I'm still only halfway through it.
e: An activity that began in the past and is still going on (since 0700): present perfect continuous.

q: You're still under that truck? How long ______ on that engine now?
e: 'How long' + an activity still in progress now = present perfect continuous (have you been working).

q: This is the third time this month that the generator ______ during a storm.
e: 'This is the first / second / third time (that)...' is followed by the present perfect.

q: Captain Reyes ______ the company for only two months, but the soldiers already trust her completely.
e: A situation that started in the past and is still true now ('already trust') takes the present perfect with 'for'.

q: Look at the runway lights; they ______ on and off like that for the last ten minutes.
e: 'For the last ten minutes' + an action still happening now = present perfect continuous.

q: I can't believe how much this town ______ since I was first stationed here in 2015.
e: Main clause with 'since + past time' = present perfect; the since-clause itself stays in the simple past.

q: I ______ much sleep lately because of the night shifts, so I'm drinking way too much coffee.
e: 'Lately' goes with the present perfect (continuous) for a recent situation that continues now.

q: So far this week, Corporal Diaz ______ twelve job applications, but nobody has called him back.
e: A number of finished items (twelve) + 'so far' = present perfect simple, not continuous.

q: My knee ______ since the road march on Tuesday, so I've made an appointment at the clinic.
e: A situation continuing from a past point (Tuesday) up to now: present perfect continuous.

q: Honestly, this is the best barbecue I ______ since I left Texas three years ago.
e: Superlative + experience up to now ('since I left'): the present perfect (the best I have had).

q: The price of fuel ______ steadily over the past six months, and drivers are starting to feel it.
e: 'Over the past six months' + a trend still going on now = present perfect continuous.

q: Has anyone seen my ID card? I ______ it somewhere, and I can't get into the building without it.
e: A past action with a result now (I can't get in): present perfect.

q: I ______ in Germany for three years as a kid, but I ______ back since.
e: A finished period in the past (as a kid) takes the simple past; 'since' (up to now) takes the present perfect.

q: We ______ for the bus for forty minutes when a staff car finally stopped and offered us a ride.
e: Duration of an action up to a moment in the past (when the car stopped): past perfect continuous.

q: My locker was wide open when I got back to the barracks; someone ______ it while I was at the range.
e: An action completed before another past moment (when I got back): past perfect, active voice.

q: The pilot admitted that until that day he ______ that type of aircraft only once.
e: Experience up to a past point ('until that day') in reported speech: past perfect.

q: By the age of thirty, my grandfather ______ in two wars and earned three medals for bravery.
e: 'By + a past point' takes the past perfect: had fought ... and (had) earned.

q: Her eyes were red and sore because she ______ at a computer screen for twelve hours straight.
e: A long earlier activity that explains a past result (red eyes): past perfect continuous.

q: It was the first time the recruits ______ live ammunition, and some of them were visibly nervous.
e: 'It was the first time (that)...' is followed by the past perfect, active voice here.

q: I barely recognized Major Tran at the reunion; he ______ a lot of weight since our academy days.
e: A change completed before a past moment (the reunion), counted 'since' an earlier time: past perfect.

q: Yesterday the mechanics finally found and repaired the leak that ______ oil onto the hangar floor for weeks.
e: The leak was fixed yesterday, so its weeks of dripping lead up to a past point: past perfect continuous.

q: How long ______ in Italy before you were transferred to Texas?
e: Duration up to an earlier past event (before you were transferred): past perfect.

q: The interpreter apologized for being late, explaining that her flight ______ in Chicago for three hours.
e: Passive past perfect: the flight was delayed (by something else) before she apologized.

q: Until he joined the Navy at nineteen, Ray ______ the ocean; he grew up on a farm in Kansas.
e: 'Until + a past event' with an experience before that time: past perfect (had never seen).

q: When we finally reached the summit, the clouds ______, and we could see for miles in every direction.
e: The clouds cleared before we reached the summit: past perfect for the earlier past action.

q: The suspect claimed he ______ at home all evening, but the security cameras told a different story.
e: A past claim about an earlier time is backshifted to the past perfect: had been.

q: When I ______ the office, I realized I ______ my laptop on the bus.
e: Simple past for the main past events; past perfect for the earlier action (leaving the laptop).

q: At 0300 tomorrow, while most of you are asleep, the convoy ______ quietly along Route 9 toward the training area.
e: An action in progress at a precise future moment: future continuous (will be moving).

q: If all goes according to plan, by the end of this course you ______ more than 200 hours of English instruction.
e: 'By the end of' + a future time = future perfect (completed before that point).

q: When the new hangar finally opens next spring, the engineers ______ on it for almost three years.
e: Duration of an activity up to a future point: future perfect continuous.

q: Don't worry if you can't reach me tonight; I ______ to Seoul all night, and my phone will be off.
e: An action in progress throughout a future period (all night): future continuous.

q: The technicians ______ the network all weekend, so expect some outages until Monday morning.
e: An activity in progress over a future period (all weekend): future continuous.

q: Will you ______ the car this afternoon? If not, I'd like to borrow it to go to the PX.
e: Future continuous is used to ask politely about someone's plans: Will you be using...?

q: Don't worry about the leftovers; by tomorrow morning the kids ______ every last bite.
e: 'By + a future time' = future perfect (the action will be finished before then).

q: This time next week, we ______ on a beach in Florida instead of shoveling snow in Michigan.
e: 'This time next week' + an action in progress = future continuous; 'lie' means to rest.

q: By 2032, if the plan works, electric vehicles ______ most of the old gas-powered trucks on this base.
e: 'By + a future date' = future perfect for a change that will be complete.

q: When you get home, the kids ______, so please try not to slam the door.
e: An action in progress at a future moment (when you get home): future continuous.

q: The lecture starts at 0900, so if you don't get there until 0930, the speaker ______ for half an hour.
e: Duration up to a future moment (0930): future perfect continuous.

q: Next Friday my parents ______ married for forty years, so we're throwing them a surprise party.
e: A state lasting up to a future date: future perfect (will have been married for...).

q: Don't plan on leaving at 1700; the inspection ______ by then, so we'll all still be here.
e: Negative future perfect: something will not be complete by a future time (by then).

q: Don't bother calling the office after lunch; everyone ______ in the fire drill until at least three o'clock.
e: An activity in progress over a future period (until three): future continuous.

q: I ______ call you last night to wish you luck, but by the time I got off duty it was after midnight.
e: 'Was going to' expresses a past plan that did not happen.

q: The supply sergeant promised that the new uniforms ______ before the parade, but they arrived a week late.
e: Future in the past after 'promised': would + passive infinitive (uniforms are delivered by someone).

q: We were just ______ leave when the power went out, so we stayed to help light the lanterns.
e: 'Be about to + verb' = to be on the point of doing something; 'was/were about to' is its past form.

q: Little did we know that this small posting ______ the start of a thirty-year career in the Coast Guard.
e: A future event seen from the past: would (future in the past).

q: The meeting ______ at 0900, but it was pushed back because the colonel's flight was delayed.
e: 'Was supposed to + verb' = a past arrangement that did not happen as planned.

q: The ferry was to ______ at noon, but a storm kept it in port until evening.
e: 'Was to have + past participle' = a planned past event that did not take place.

q: When I talked to Ana on Monday, she said she ______ to Denver the following week for a conference.
e: A reported arrangement seen from the past: 'I'm flying' becomes 'she was flying ... the following week'.

q: I knew the final exam ______ difficult, so I studied every evening for a month.
e: After a past verb (knew), a future idea is expressed with would.

q: Sergeant Lee was on the point of ______ his resignation when the general offered him a promotion instead.
e: 'Be on the point of + -ing' = be about to do something.

q: I had a feeling it ______ rain, so I packed my poncho, and I'm glad I did.
e: A prediction made in the past: was going to (the past of 'is going to').

q: I thought you ______ the night shift this week. What are you doing here at noon?
e: After 'I thought', a planned arrangement is backshifted to the past continuous.

q: The ceremony ______ held outdoors, but because of the thunderstorm it was moved to the gym.
e: 'Was to have been + past participle' = a planned arrangement that was later changed.

q: She assured us that by Friday she ______ all the paperwork, but on Friday nothing was ready.
e: Future perfect in the past: would have + past participle (completion by a time that is now past).

q: The new bridge *was to* open in May, but the opening was delayed until fall.
e: 'Was to + verb' describes a past plan or schedule: it was scheduled to open.

q: By the time you read this email, I ______ the base and started my new job in Virginia.
e: 'By the time + present' (future meaning) takes the future perfect: will have left ... and (will have) started.

q: How many countries ______ by the time you finish your tour with the embassy?
e: Question form of the future perfect with 'by the time': will you have + past participle.

q: By the time the ambulance arrived, the injured hiker ______ in the snow for nearly three hours.
e: Duration up to a past moment: past perfect continuous; 'lie' (rest), not 'lay' (put).

q: Hurry up! By the time we ______ to the stadium, the game will have started.
e: In a 'by the time' clause about the future, use the simple present, not will.

q: By the time I ______ my coffee, the meeting had already moved on to the next item on the agenda.
e: In a past story the 'by the time' clause takes the simple past; the main clause has the past perfect.

q: By the time the medics reached the crash site, a local farmer ______ the driver out of the burning car.
e: An action completed before another past event (the medics' arrival): past perfect.

q: By the time she retires next year, Dr. Patel ______ more than 40,000 patients at this clinic.
e: 'By the time + future event' + a completed total: future perfect.

q: By the time I got to the airport, my flight ______, so I had to spend the night in the terminal.
e: 'By the time + simple past' takes the past perfect in the main clause.

q: By the time the snowplow cleared the road, we ______ in the car for six hours, singing to stay awake.
e: A state lasting up to a past moment ('for six hours'): past perfect.

q: By the time the report reaches the general's desk, most of its figures ______ out of date.
e: 'By the time + present' refers to the future, so the main clause takes will.

q: By the time the doctors identified the virus, it ______ to three other states.
e: Completed before a past event (identification): past perfect.

q: By the time I was twelve, I ______ to six different schools because my dad was in the Air Force.
e: 'By the time + past' + experience up to that point: past perfect (had been to).

q: By the time the movie ended, half the audience ______ asleep.
e: Past perfect = had + past participle (fall, fell, fallen).

q: By the time the relief crew lands, the night team ______ for fourteen hours without a break.
e: Duration up to a future moment (when the crew lands): future perfect continuous.

q: By the time the inspectors ______, we ______ every vehicle in the motor pool.
e: No will after 'by the time' (simple present for the future); the main clause takes the future perfect.

q: Ever since the new road ______, traffic past the main gate has more than doubled.
e: 'Since' + a point in the past takes the simple past; the main clause takes the present perfect.

q: It's been almost a year ______ I last saw my brother, who is deployed overseas.
e: It's been + a period + since + simple past (from that moment until now).

q: I haven't had a single soda ______ my annual physical in March, and I've already lost eight pounds.
e: 'Since' + a point in time (my physical in March); 'for' needs a length of time.

q: The two pilots met at flight school twenty years ______, and they have been close friends ever since.
e: 'Ago' counts back from now and goes with the simple past (met).

q: How long has it been since you last ______ a real vacation with your family?
e: 'Since you last + simple past' marks the last time something happened.

q: Corporal Burke ______ in the motor pool for six months before he moved to the communications section.
e: 'For' does not always need the present perfect: a finished past period takes the simple past.

q: I sprained my ankle in May and haven't been able to run ______.
e: 'Since' can end a sentence as an adverb meaning 'from then until now'.

q: That apartment ______ empty since the Garcias moved to Ohio last spring.
e: From a past point (since ... last spring) up to now: present perfect.

q: I've known Tom since we ______ in basic training together.
e: After 'since' the clause names a past time, so it uses the simple past.

q: It ______ ten years since the base hospital was last renovated, and it really shows.
e: It has been + a period + since + simple past (American English: It's been ten years since...).

q: We ______ each other for only a few weeks when we got engaged, and our friends thought we were crazy.
e: Duration up to a past event (getting engaged): past perfect; 'know' is not used in continuous forms.

q: How long ago ______ the base gym? It still looks brand new.
e: 'Ago' takes the simple past; in a question use did + subject + base verb.

q: Our family has lived in Colorado Springs since ______, when my father was assigned to Fort Carson.
e: 'Since' needs a point in time (2019); 'for' goes with a length of time.

q: The printer on the second floor ______ for weeks, but nobody has bothered to report it.
e: A repeated problem from weeks ago until now: present perfect continuous with 'for'.

q: When I was first stationed in Alaska, I couldn't ______ the long winter nights.
e: 'Get used to + noun' = become accustomed to; after couldn't use the base form 'get'.

q: After ten years in the Marines, my brother ______ to getting up before dawn.
e: 'Be used to + -ing' = be accustomed to something.

q: There ______ a movie theater on this corner, but it closed down years ago.
e: 'Used to + base verb' describes a past situation that is no longer true.

q: I ______ drink so much coffee before I started working night shifts.
e: Negative of 'used to': didn't use to + base verb (no -d after did).

q: Living in a small apartment was hard at first, but we've gotten used to ______ in tight spaces.
e: In 'get used to', 'to' is a preposition, so it is followed by the -ing form.

q: Every Sunday after dinner, my grandfather ______ tell us stories about his years in the Navy.
e: 'Would + base verb' describes repeated past actions (like 'used to').

q: Coming from London, Emma found it hard to ______ on the right side of the road.
e: 'Get used to + -ing' = become accustomed to doing something.

q: Where ______ live before you moved to Texas?
e: Question form of 'used to': did + subject + use to + base verb.

q: Our old drill sergeant was strict, so we ______ being yelled at for the smallest mistakes.
e: 'Be used to + -ing' = be accustomed to; 'used to' alone would need a base verb.

q: When we were kids, we ______ a dog named Rocket who followed us everywhere.
e: For past states (have, own, live) use 'used to'; 'would' is only for repeated actions.

q: It took Ahmed a few months, but eventually he ______ the American habit of tipping in restaurants.
e: 'Get used to + noun' describes the process of becoming accustomed.

q: She ______ a lot when she was younger, but now she hardly ever leaves her hometown.
e: 'Used to + base verb' = a past habit that has stopped.

q: Didn't you ______ in the same unit as my cousin Mike?
e: After did/didn't, write 'use to' + base verb (Didn't you use to serve...?).

q: As a young lieutenant, Colonel Hayes *would* run five miles before breakfast every day.
e: 'Would' for a repeated past action has the same meaning as 'used to'.

q: After six months at the embassy, Lieutenant Moss *has adjusted to* the slower pace of life.
e: 'Adjust to' = become accustomed to = get used to (American English: has gotten used to).

q: If the sergeant had renewed his passport last month, he ______ with the advance team right now.
e: Mixed conditional: past condition (had renewed) + present result (would be + -ing, 'right now').

q: If Lieutenant Park ______ so afraid of heights, she would have volunteered for the airborne course years ago.
e: Mixed conditional: a present, permanent trait (if + were/weren't) + a past result (would have volunteered).

q: We ______ lost in the desert now if you had listened to the guide this morning.
e: Past condition (had listened) with a present result ('now'): would/wouldn't + base verb.

q: If the engineers were more careful, the bridge ______ during last week's flood.
e: Present unreal condition (general carelessness) + past result: would have + past participle.

q: Had the doctor not noticed the symptoms early, Corporal Diaz ______ still in the hospital today.
e: Inverted past condition (Had ... not noticed) + present result ('today'): would be.

q: If I spoke Arabic, I ______ for the liaison job in Qatar last year.
e: Present unreal fact (I don't speak Arabic) + past result: would have been + past participle (passive).

q: If I had saved more money when I was single, I ______ about these car payments now.
e: Past condition + present result ('now'): would (not) be + -ing.

q: If it weren't for the new GPS units, we ______ hopelessly lost on yesterday's night march.
e: If it weren't for (= without, present) + a result in the past (yesterday): would have + past participle.

q: If the major ______ the budget request last spring, we would have new radios by now.
e: An unreal past event (last spring) needs the past perfect in the if-clause, even when the result is present.

q: Mike ______ the promotion board last year if he weren't so disorganized.
e: Present trait (weren't so disorganized) + past result (last year): would have passed.

q: She ______ fluent in French by now if she had stayed in Paris after the exchange program.
e: Mixed conditional: past condition (had stayed) + present result (by now): would be.

q: *Had it not been for the medic*, the patrol leader would not be alive today.
o: If the medic had not been there
Because the medic had not been there
e: Had it not been for X = If X had not been there / without X (inverted past condition).

q: If you didn't owe the credit union so much money, you ______ that new truck last weekend.
e: Present situation (you owe money) + past result (last weekend): could have + past participle.

q: If our unit had moved to Alaska last year, my kids ______ to the snow by now.
e: Past condition + present state: would be used to (= accustomed to) the snow now.

q: What would you be doing now if you ______ the Army?
e: Joining the Army is a past event, so the if-clause takes the past perfect; the result is present (would be doing now).

q: I'm not a morning person; otherwise I ______ for the 0500 run yesterday.
e: Otherwise = if I were a morning person (present) + past result (yesterday): would have signed up.

q: If he were a better listener, he ______ the instructions the first time, and we wouldn't be repeating them now.
e: Present trait (were a better listener) + past result (the first time): would have understood.

q: If the alarm system were more reliable, ______ the break-in last night?
e: Present condition + past result in a question: would + subject + have + past participle.

q: If I hadn't broken my ankle last month, I ______ in next week's marathon.
e: Past condition (hadn't broken) + future result that is now impossible: would be + -ing.

q: Supposing you had been born in Germany, what language ______ at home now?
e: Supposing + past perfect (past condition) + present result (now): would you speak.

q: Not until the last vehicle had crossed the river ______ the engineers allowed to remove the bridge.
e: Not until + clause, then inversion in the main clause: were the engineers allowed (passive).

q: Little ______ that the inspection team was already waiting in his office.
e: Little at the start (= not at all) takes auxiliary inversion: Little did he know ...

q: So heavy ______ that the flight to Anchorage was canceled.
e: So + adjective at the start of the sentence: invert be and the subject (So heavy was the snowfall that ...).

q: Only by working through the night ______ the deadline.
e: Only by + -ing at the start triggers inversion with do/does/did: Only by ... did the team meet.

q: At no time ______ allowed to take classified files out of this room.
e: At no time is already negative and takes inversion: At no time are visitors allowed (no second 'not').

q: No sooner ______ the new schedule than the commander changed it again.
e: No sooner at the start: inversion with the past perfect (No sooner had we received ... than ...).

q: Seldom ______ a recruit finish the obstacle course in under four minutes.
e: Seldom at the start takes inversion; present simple with a singular subject: does a recruit finish.

q: Not only ______ late for formation, but she also forgot her ID card.
e: Not only at the start: invert the verb be and the subject (was she late), not did.

q: On no account ______ the generator be switched off during the night.
e: On no account is already negative: inversion with a positive modal (should the generator be ...).

q: Scarcely ______ my boots off when the phone rang again.
e: Scarcely ... when: inversion with the past perfect (Scarcely had I taken ...).

q: Never in the battalion's history ______ so many soldiers earned the expert badge in a single day.
e: Never at the start: inversion; present perfect with a plural subject (have ... soldiers earned).

q: The pilot checked the fuel twice. Only then ______ the engines.
e: Only then at the start takes inversion with did + base verb: Only then did she start.

q: ______ the weather improve, the jump will go ahead as planned.
e: Should + subject + base verb = If the weather improves (formal conditional inversion).

q: ______ the convoy to leave now, it would reach the border before dark.
e: Were + subject + to-infinitive = If the convoy left now (hypothetical present/future).

q: Such ______ the noise from the generators that nobody could sleep.
e: Such + be + subject + that: Such was the noise that ... (be agrees with 'the noise').

q: Nowhere ______ a better place to learn mountain warfare than at this school.
e: Negative adverb Nowhere at the start: inversion with the auxiliary (will you find).

q: In no way ______ responsible for the damage to the rental car.
e: In no way at the start: invert be and the subject (is the driver responsible).

q: *Little did we know* that the exercise would last three more days.
e: Little did we know = we had no idea at all (emphatic inversion).

q: The plane had ______ taken off when the pilot reported an engine problem.
e: had hardly + past participle ... when (without inversion); 'no sooner' needs 'than', and 'hardly ever' means 'almost never'.

q: ______ the mechanic checked the brakes before the trip, the truck wouldn't be in the ditch now.
e: Had + subject + past participle = If the mechanic had checked (past condition), with a present result (now).

q: The ground is completely dry, so it ______ last night after all.
e: can't have + past participle: a logical conclusion that something did not happen in the past.

q: You *needn't have cooked*; we already ate at the dining facility.
o: It wasn't necessary, but you did it
You weren't allowed to cook for us
You probably didn't do any cooking
You should have cooked something else
e: needn't have + past participle: the action was done, but it was not necessary.

q: The forecast was clear, so I ______ an umbrella and left it at home.
e: didn't need to = it was not necessary and I did not do it; needn't have taken would mean I took it.

q: The guard ______ asleep at his post; the officer on duty heard him snoring.
e: must have been: a confident deduction about the past from evidence (snoring).

q: The report ______ by the time the general arrived, but the printer broke down.
e: should have been + past participle: past passive expectation that did not happen.

q: I ______ to the wedding, but I was on duty that weekend.
e: would have liked to + base verb: a past wish that was not fulfilled.

q: It's getting dark. We ______ head back to camp before the trail gets dangerous.
e: had better + base verb gives strong advice for now ('We'd better').

q: The lieutenant ______ have finished the course in record time; he was injured halfway through.
e: can't have + past participle: impossible in the past (he was injured).

q: When I was a cadet, we ______ run five miles before breakfast every Saturday.
e: would + base verb describes a repeated past action (like 'used to').

q: Fortunately, the pilot ______ land the damaged plane safely on the highway.
e: For one specific success in the past, use was able to (managed to), not affirmative could.

q: The light in the supply office was still on at 0300, so the clerk ______ late.
e: must have been + -ing: a deduction about an action in progress in the past.

q: Why did you take a taxi? I ______ you up at the airport.
e: could have + past participle: a past possibility that was not used.

q: The package ______ arrived by now; it was shipped two weeks ago.
e: should have + past participle (by now): what we expect to have happened already.

q: Don't worry about the exam. With all your preparation, you ______ pass easily.
e: be bound to + base verb = be certain to.

q: The meeting ______ at 0900 yesterday, but the colonel's flight was delayed.
e: was supposed to + base verb: a past plan or arrangement that did not happen.

q: You ______ as well take the stairs; the elevator has been out of order for a week.
e: might as well + base verb: there is no better option, so do it.

q: That ______ Sergeant Kim at the door; she said she'd stop by around six.
e: must be: a confident present deduction; 'can' is not used for a specific deduction.

q: The keys ______ in the truck; I can see them hanging from the ignition.
e: must have been + past participle: a passive deduction about the past (someone left them).

q: We ______ wait for the bus; Dan has offered to drive us.
e: don't need to = it is not necessary; 'mustn't' is a prohibition, and 'needn't' takes no 'to'.

q: Be careful with that ladder! You ______ fallen and broken your neck.
e: might have + past participle: something that was possible but did not happen.

q: ______ the report, the captain signed it and sent it to headquarters.
e: Having + past participle (active): one action finished before the next one.

q: ______ in 1942, the airfield is still used for training flights today.
e: A past participle clause has a passive meaning: the airfield was built in 1942.

q: ______ twice for promotion, the sergeant finally decided to retire.
e: Perfect passive participle: Having been + past participle (he was passed over before he decided).

q: ______ no money left, the young private called his parents for help.
e: A present participle clause gives the reason: Having no money = Because he had no money.

q: Not ______ the area before, the patrol relied completely on their local guide.
e: Negative perfect participle: Not having + past participle = because they had not visited.

q: The soldiers ______ in the accident were flown to the hospital in Landstuhl.
e: Reduced relative clause with a past participle: the soldiers (who were) injured in the accident.

q: Anyone ______ to attend the ceremony must register with the front office by Friday.
e: Reduced relative clause with -ing: anyone (who wishes) = anyone wishing.

q: ______ his ID card at home, Specialist Ruiz was not allowed onto the base.
e: Having + past participle (active) gives an earlier action that explains the result.

q: Having finished the inspection of the motor pool, ______.
o: lunch was served to the general
it was time for the general's lunch
e: The subject of the main clause must be the person who did the participle action (the general finished).

q: The letter, ______ in haste, contained several spelling mistakes.
e: Past participle clause with a passive meaning: the letter, (which was) written in haste.

q: ______ by the noise, the dog began to bark wildly.
e: Past participle for a passive meaning: the dog was frightened by the noise.

q: With smoke ______ from the engine, the pilot headed for the nearest field.
e: with + noun + -ing describes an action happening at the same time (smoke was pouring).

q: ______ from his accent, the new instructor grew up somewhere near Boston.
e: Judging from/by is a fixed participle phrase meaning 'based on what we can see or hear'.

q: ______ in the field for six weeks, the unit was given a long weekend.
e: Having + past participle (active): the unit served first, then got the weekend off.

q: The woman ______ next to the colonel is our new interpreter.
e: Reduced relative clause: the woman (who is) standing next to the colonel.

q: Most of the equipment ______ to the unit last year has already broken down.
e: Reduced relative clause with a past participle: the equipment (that was) issued to the unit.

q: ______ unable to contact headquarters, the lieutenant made the decision herself.
e: Being + adjective gives the reason: Because she was unable to contact headquarters.

q: When ______ by reporters, soldiers should refer all questions to the public affairs office.
e: When + past participle (passive): when (they are) approached by reporters.

q: Not ______ what to say, the new recruit just nodded and smiled.
e: Not + -ing gives the reason: because he did not know what to say.

q: *Having been warned about the ice*, the drivers slowed down on the mountain road.
o: Because someone had warned them about the ice
Although they had warned others about the ice
While they were warning others about the ice
Before anyone warned them about the ice
e: Having been + past participle = because they had been warned (passive, earlier action).

q: What surprised everyone ______ how quickly the new recruit learned the procedures.
e: What-cleft: What + clause + be + focus (What surprised everyone was ...).

q: It was the medic, not the doctor, ______ saved the soldier's life.
e: It-cleft for a person in subject position: It was ... who (or that) ...

q: ______ I don't understand is why the meeting was moved again.
e: What-cleft: What I don't understand is ... (What = the thing that).

q: All I want after this deployment ______ a long, hot shower.
e: All-cleft: All I want is ... (All = the only thing), with a singular verb.

q: What the recruits ______ was march twenty miles with full packs.
e: What-cleft with an action: What + subject + did / had to do + was + base verb.

q: It wasn't until we reached the base ______ that one of the radios was missing.
e: It was not until ... that ...: the cleft uses 'that' and normal word order (no inversion).

q: The reason ______ I joined the Navy is that I wanted to see the world.
e: The reason why ... is that ...: 'why' (or 'that') follows 'the reason', not 'because'.

q: It ______ the new radios that caused all the problems during the exercise.
e: In an it-cleft the verb after 'it' is always singular: It was the radios that ...

q: ______ was his calm voice that kept the passengers from panicking.
e: It-cleft to emphasize one element: It was his calm voice that ...

q: What happened ______ that the truck ran out of fuel ten miles from camp.
e: What happened was (that) ...: a what-cleft that presents an event.

q: The person ______ you should talk to is Master Sergeant Bell.
e: Cleft with 'the person who': the person who you should talk to is ...

q: Forget the new equipment; what ______ more time to train.
e: What-cleft: what + subject + verb (no inversion) + is; 'time' is uncountable, so 'is'.

q: Nobody called the police. What they did was ______ the whole thing on their phones.
e: What + subject + did + was + base verb (or to-infinitive): What they did was film ...

q: I didn't lose my wallet. What ______ leave it in the taxi.
e: What-cleft with an action: What I did was + base verb.

q: The thing ______ worries me is the lack of spare parts.
e: The thing that ... is ...: 'that' (not 'what') follows a noun.

q: It's not the money ______ I care about; it's the time away from my family.
e: It-cleft with a thing as focus: It's not the money that ...

q: It was ______ the end of the exercise that we finally got some sleep.
e: It was not until + time + that ... = only at that time and not before.

q: It was because of the fog ______ the flight was delayed.
e: It-cleft focusing on a reason: It was because of ... that ...

q: It's the little things ______ make the biggest difference on a long deployment.
e: It-cleft with a plural focus: It's the little things that make ... ('that', not 'what').

q: The place ______ I feel most relaxed is my grandfather's cabin in Montana.
e: The place where ... is ...: 'where' introduces a place in a cleft-type sentence.

q: Help ______ to more coffee; there's plenty left in the pot.
e: When the object is the same person as the subject (here the 'you' of the imperative), use the reflexive pronoun: help yourself.

q: This canteen isn't mine; it must be ______.
e: A possessive pronoun standing alone is 'hers' (no apostrophe); 'her' needs a noun after it.

q: The medic said it would take about ______ hour to get the lab results.
e: The h in 'hour' is silent, so the word begins with a vowel sound and takes 'an'.

q: Sergeant Brooks earns about $3,000 ______ month, plus a housing allowance.
e: For a rate per unit of time, 'a' means 'per': $3,000 a month.

q: The base library is ______ only place on post with free Wi-Fi.
e: 'Only' makes the noun unique, so it takes 'the': the only place.

q: Could you give me ______ advice about preparing for the ECL?
e: 'Advice' is uncountable: no a/an and no 'many'; use 'some' (or 'a piece of advice').

q: The movie theater on base is closed ______ Mondays and Tuesdays.
e: Days of the week take 'on': on Mondays.

q: Most of the cadets travel home ______ train during the holidays.
e: Means of transportation without an article takes 'by': by train ('on the train' needs the article).

q: This rifle is similar ______ the one we used in basic training.
e: The adjective 'similar' is followed by 'to'.

q: Are you still afraid ______ flying after that rough landing?
e: 'Afraid of' + noun or -ing form: afraid of flying.

q: The bus to the airport leaves ______ ten minutes, so grab your bag.
e: 'In' + a period of time = at the end of that period from now: in ten minutes.

q: The convoy ______ the main gate about twenty minutes ago.
e: 'Ago' marks a finished time in the past, so use the simple past, not the present perfect.

q: Sergeant Young ______ in the Army for twelve years, and he plans to stay for eight more.
e: An action that began in the past and is still going on, with 'for' + a period: present perfect.

q: When we reached the mess hall, the lunch line ______ already.
e: An action completed before another past action takes the past perfect.

q: He promised he ______ us at the gate at 0600, but he never showed up.
e: Future in the past after a past reporting verb: would + base verb.

q: Don't leave the motor pool until the mechanic ______ the brakes.
e: After time words such as 'until', 'when' and 'as soon as', use a present tense for a future action, not 'will'.

q: Be quiet! The lieutenant ______ on the phone with the colonel.
e: An action happening at the moment of speaking takes the present continuous.

q: Corporal Ruiz ______ the floor when the inspector walked in.
e: An action in progress when another past action interrupted it takes the past continuous.

q: Look at those dark clouds; it ______ rain any minute now.
e: A prediction based on what you can see now: be going to + base verb.

q: Between you and ______, I don't think the exercise will start on time.
e: After a preposition (between), use an object pronoun: between you and me.

q: These boots are too tight; do you have any bigger ______?
e: 'Ones' replaces a plural countable noun (boots) after an adjective.

q: The officer ______ car was towed should report to the MP station.
e: 'Whose' shows possession (the officer's car); 'who's' means 'who is' or 'who has'.

q: The battalion is proud of ______ long history.
e: The possessive 'its' has no apostrophe; 'it's' means 'it is' or 'it has'.

q: ______ soldier in the company has to qualify on the range this month.
e: 'Every' + singular noun + singular verb; 'all', 'most' and 'both' need a plural noun.

q: How ______ luggage are you allowed to bring on the flight?
e: 'Luggage' is uncountable, so ask 'how much'.

q: If the fuel in the generator ______ below a quarter tank, the backup system switches on automatically.
e: Zero conditional for an automatic result: if + present simple, present simple.

q: If the replacement parts haven't arrived by Thursday, we ______ the convoy until next week.
e: First conditional: a real future possibility (if + present perfect) takes will + verb in the main clause.

q: If you ______ run into Sergeant Diaz at the PX, could you remind him about tomorrow's formation?
e: If you happen to + verb = if by chance you...; no will or would in the if-clause.

q: Water pipes in the old barracks can burst if the temperature ______ below freezing for several nights in a row.
e: Real conditional: the if-clause takes the present simple, never will.

q: If you ______ your online security training by Monday, you will lose access to the network.
e: First conditional: if + present perfect (haven't completed by Monday) for a future deadline; no will in the if-clause.

q: The instructor told us that if we ______ the written test, we would be allowed to drive the trucks on the course.
e: Reported first conditional: 'If you pass, you will...' becomes 'if we passed, we would...'.

q: If anyone ______ about the schedule change, tell them to check the battalion website.
e: If + present simple with an imperative in the main clause.

q: Unless you ______ the form today, the payment ______ until next month.
e: Unless + present simple (= if you don't submit), then will + verb for the future result.

q: If the base gym ______ open twenty-four hours a day, more of us could work out after the night shift.
e: Second conditional (unreal present): if + past (were), could/would + verb.

q: If I ______ enough leave left this year, I would fly home for my sister's wedding, but I used it all in March.
e: Second conditional: an unreal present situation takes the past simple (had) in the if-clause.

q: If the enemy ______ the bridge tonight, our only route to the airfield would be cut off.
e: If + were to + verb presents an unlikely future event; the result uses would.

q: What ______ you do if you found a wallet full of cash in the parking lot?
e: Second conditional question: would + subject + verb ... if + past simple.

q: My brother would pass his college entrance exams easily if he ______ so much time on video games every night.
e: Second conditional (unreal present): would + verb ... if + past simple (didn't spend).

q: I ______ that phone if I were you; the reviews say the battery dies after a few hours.
e: Advice with 'if I were you': the main clause takes would + verb.

q: If we ______ speak to the pilot directly, we could sort this out in five minutes, but she's already in the air.
e: Unreal present ability: if + could + verb, then could/would + verb.

q: If it ______ so hard right now, we would be practicing on the outdoor range instead of sitting in this classroom.
e: Unreal present (right now): if + past continuous, would be + -ing.

q: If the clinic ______ better, patients wouldn't have to wait three weeks for an appointment.
e: Second conditional in the passive: if + were + past participle.

q: Would you accept the position in Alaska if they ______ it to you?
e: Second conditional question: would ... if + past simple (offered).

q: If I ______ in charge, things ______ very differently around here.
e: Second conditional: if + were (unreal present), would + verb (here passive: would be done).

q: If the pilot ______ the warning light earlier, she could have avoided the emergency landing.
e: Third conditional: if + past perfect, could have + past participle.

q: We ______ the ferry if the taxi driver hadn't taken the wrong exit.
e: Third conditional: an unreal past result takes would have + past participle.

q: If the bridge ______ properly last year, it would not have collapsed during the storm.
e: Third conditional in the passive: if + had been + past participle.

q: The patient ______ if the ambulance had arrived ten minutes later.
e: Third conditional: might have + past participle for a possible but unreal past result.

q: If you hadn't reminded me, I ______ about my dental appointment completely.
e: Third conditional: if + past perfect, would have + past participle.

q: What would you have done if the platoon sergeant ______ you asleep on guard duty?
e: Third conditional question: the if-clause takes the past perfect (had caught), not would have.

q: If the weather had been better, the climbing team ______ the summit before dark.
e: Third conditional: could have + past participle for an unreal past possibility.

q: The accident report concluded that if the driver ______ attention, he would have seen the stop sign.
e: Third conditional with an action in progress: if + had been + -ing.

q: I'm sure Maria ______ you a ride to the airport if you had asked her.
e: Third conditional: would have + past participle in the main clause.

q: If the smoke detector ______ working, the family ______ out of the house much sooner.
o: would have been ... would have gotten
e: Third conditional: if + past perfect, would have + past participle; never would have in the if-clause.

q: If I had accepted the job offer in San Diego, I ______ near the beach now.
e: Mixed conditional: past condition (had accepted), present result (would be living ... now).

q: If she hadn't broken her ankle last month, she ______ in tomorrow's marathon.
e: Mixed conditional: past cause, present/future result with would be + -ing.

q: If Corporal Lee ______ so afraid of heights, he would have volunteered for airborne school last year.
e: Mixed conditional: a permanent fact (if + past: weren't) explains a past result (would have volunteered).

q: If I spoke Spanish, I ______ the job at the embassy last spring.
e: Mixed conditional: unreal present condition (spoke), unreal past result (would have gotten).

q: We ______ lost right now if you had brought the map as I asked you to.
e: Mixed conditional: past condition (had brought), present result (wouldn't be ... right now).

q: If the engineers had designed the network properly, we ______ these outages every single day now.
e: Mixed conditional: if + past perfect, would be + -ing for a present situation (now).

q: If I ______ that second cup of coffee at midnight, I wouldn't feel so exhausted this morning.
e: Mixed conditional: past condition (hadn't drunk), present result (wouldn't feel).

q: If you had saved some of your reenlistment bonus, you ______ afford a new car now.
e: Mixed conditional: past condition, present result with could + verb (now).

q: Lisa ______ the promotion last year if she were more willing to relocate.
e: Mixed conditional: a present attitude (were more willing) explains a past result (might have gotten).

q: If the budget hadn't been cut, the base clinic ______ open on Saturdays, but now it closes at noon on Fridays.
e: Mixed conditional: past cause (hadn't been cut), present result (would still be open).

q: Where ______ today if you hadn't joined the Air Force after high school?
e: Mixed conditional question: past condition (hadn't joined), present result (would you be ... today).

q: ______ the generator fail during the night, switch to the battery packs immediately.
e: Formal inversion: Should the generator fail = If the generator fails.

q: ______ I known how heavy the traffic would be, I would have taken the train.
e: Inverted third conditional: Had I known = If I had known.

q: ______ for the new radar system, the storm would have caught the fleet by surprise.
e: Inverted third conditional: Had it not been for = If it hadn't been for.

q: Were the convoy ______ delayed, the supply point would stay open until 2200.
e: Inverted 'were to' conditional: Were the convoy to be delayed = If the convoy were (to be) delayed.

q: ______ any questions about your travel voucher, the finance office will be glad to help.
e: Should + subject + base verb (inversion) = If you have; the result is a real future.

q: Had the medic ______ so quickly, the soldier could have lost his leg.
e: Negative inverted conditional: Had + subject + not + past participle (no contraction).

q: The ceremony will be moved into the gym, ______ it rain on Saturday.
e: An inverted should-clause can follow the main clause: should it rain = if it rains.

q: Had the contract been signed in March, the new barracks ______ by now.
e: Mixed inverted conditional: past condition, present result in the passive (would be finished by now).

q: ______ your quick thinking, the fire would have spread to the ammunition storage area.
e: But for + noun = if it hadn't been for; used with a would have result.

q: If it ______ for my parents' support, I could never have finished college while working full time.
e: If it hadn't been for + noun = without that help in the past; the result is could have + past participle.

q: ______ GPS, most of us would be completely lost in an unfamiliar city.
e: Without + noun can replace an if-clause: Without GPS = If we didn't have GPS.

q: If it ______ for the air conditioning, nobody could work in this office in August.
e: If it weren't for + noun = without (unreal present); the result uses could/would.

q: I wish I ______ how to fix this printer; the IT office is closed until Monday.
e: Wish about a present situation: wish + past simple.

q: I wish I ______ my phone charger at the hotel; now I have no way to call home.
e: Regret about the past: wish + past perfect.

q: I wish the people upstairs ______ furniture around at two in the morning.
e: Wish + would expresses annoyance at someone's repeated behavior.

q: Our son wishes he ______ come home for the reunion, but his ship doesn't return until June.
e: Wish + could for an ability or possibility that does not exist now.

q: If only we ______ the truck's tires before the road trip; we had a blowout twenty miles outside Denver.
e: If only + past perfect = strong regret about the past.

q: If only this office ______ a window; I haven't seen daylight since 0700.
e: If only + past simple = a wish about the present.

q: Sometimes I wish my job ______ a little less predictable.
e: Wish + were (subjunctive) for an unreal present situation.

q: I wish the commander ______ a decision about the deployment dates soon; the whole unit is waiting.
e: Wish + would + verb for a change we want someone else to make in the future.

q: The soldiers wish they ______ about the schedule change before they bought their plane tickets.
e: Past regret in the passive: wish + had been + past participle.

q: She wishes she ______ her grandmother one last time before she passed away.
e: Wish + could have + past participle: regret about a past possibility.

q: *I wish I hadn't volunteered* for the weekend shift.
e: Wish + past perfect expresses regret about something that already happened.

q: If only the rain ______; we've been stuck in our tents for three days.
e: If only + would: an impatient wish for a change in the near future.

q: I wish I ______ harder in high school; if I had, I ______ a better job now.
e: Wish + past perfect (past regret), then a mixed conditional: if I had, I would have ... now.

q: The aircraft cannot take off unless the crosswind ______ below twenty-five knots.
e: Unless = if ... not; it takes the present simple and no extra negative.

q: ______ you have a valid ID card, the guards at the gate will not let you on post.
e: Unless = except if: no ID, no entry.

q: Don't wake the duty officer ______ it's a real emergency.
e: Unless = except if; only a real emergency is a reason to wake him.

q: Unless the lab results ______ any problems, you can return to full duty on Monday.
e: Unless already means 'if not', so the verb stays affirmative; present simple for the future.

q: *Unless the parts arrive tomorrow*, the repairs will be delayed again.
o: If the parts don't arrive tomorrow
Even if the parts arrive tomorrow
As soon as the parts arrive tomorrow
e: Unless + affirmative verb = if + negative verb.

q: We'll go hiking on Sunday *unless it rains*.
e: Unless it rains = if it doesn't rain.

q: Hand in your expense reports by the 15th; ______, you will have to wait another month for your money.
e: Otherwise = if not (if you don't); it links two sentences.

q: I wouldn't drive on these icy roads unless it ______ absolutely necessary.
e: Unless in a second conditional: unless + past (were) = if it weren't.

q: You may use the government vehicle for the trip ______ you return it with a full tank.
e: Provided (that) = on condition that.

q: ______ you keep the receipt, you can return the boots within thirty days.
e: As long as = provided that / on condition that.

q: The trip to the coast is still on as long as the weather ______ good.
e: As long as (condition) takes the present simple for the future, not will.

q: Provided that the medical board ______ her, Sergeant Ortiz will return to flight status next month.
e: Provided that + present simple for a future condition.

q: The landlord will lower the rent on condition that we ______ a two-year lease.
e: On condition that + present simple for a future condition.

q: Only if the bridge is repaired ______ this route again.
e: Only if + clause at the start causes inversion in the main clause: will the convoy use.

q: The mission will go ahead tomorrow ______ it rains; the weather is not going to stop us.
e: Even if = whether or not; the result does not change.

q: *As long as* you follow the safety rules, the range is a safe place to train.
o: In spite of the fact that
e: As long as (condition) = provided that.

q: Small-arms qualification will take place on Range 7 ______ the range safety officer is available.
e: Providing (that) = provided that = on condition that.

q: Write the access code down ______ you forget it.
e: In case = as a precaution because something might happen.

q: I'll pack my rain jacket in case it ______ during the hike.
e: In case + present simple for a future possibility; no will.

q: Last night she left the porch light on in case her husband ______ home late from the night shift.
e: In a past context, in case is followed by the past simple.

q: ______ a power outage, the hospital's emergency generators start within ten seconds.
e: In case of + noun = in the event of; in case alone is followed by a clause.

q: Here is my cell number, in case you ______ need to reach me over the weekend.
e: In case you should + verb is a formal way to show the event is not very likely; will is not used after in case.

q: Last summer we stored extra drinking water ______ the well ran dry.
e: In case = as a precaution against something that might happen.

q: The pilots carry survival kits *in case* they have to eject over the ocean.
e: In case = as a precaution because something might happen.

q: Take the night-vision goggles with you, just ______.
e: Just in case can end a sentence: as a precaution.

q: The colonel insisted that every officer ______ present at the safety briefing.
e: Subjunctive after insist (a demand): base form 'be' for every subject.

q: It is essential that the patient ______ anything after midnight before the surgery.
e: Negative subjunctive: that + subject + not + base form.

q: The inspector recommended that the old wiring ______ before winter.
e: Passive subjunctive after recommend: be + past participle.

q: The workers are demanding that the company ______ its decision to close the factory.
e: Subjunctive after demand: base form (reverse), even with a singular subject.

q: My advice? I'd suggest that your son ______ for the scholarship before the March deadline.
e: Suggest that + subject + base form (subjunctive).

q: It's high time you ______ your car registration; it expired in June.
e: It's (high) time + subject + past simple = this should already be done.

q: I'd rather you ______ the kids about the move until we know the exact date.
e: Would rather + another subject + past simple for a present or future wish.

q: The general's request that the ceremony ______ short was politely ignored by every speaker.
e: A noun like request or demand + that takes the subjunctive: be kept.

q: The medic insisted that I ______ my boots back on until the swelling went down.
e: Negative subjunctive after insist: not + base form.

q: It is imperative that every passenger ______ the aircraft before refueling begins.
e: It is imperative that + base form (subjunctive) for all subjects.

q: The old barracks ______ down last month, and a new fitness center is going up in their place.
e: Past simple passive (were + past participle) with a finished time ('last month'); the present perfect cannot go with 'last month'.

q: Please use the side entrance this week; the main lobby ______.
e: Present continuous passive (is being + past participle) for work in progress now; the lobby does not paint anything.

q: When the inspection team arrived, the trucks ______, so the sergeant asked the team to wait twenty minutes.
e: Past continuous passive (were being + past participle): an action in progress at a past moment, done to the trucks.

q: By the time the medics reached the village, the injured ______ to a clinic by local volunteers.
e: Past perfect passive (had been + past participle): finished before another past event; 'by local volunteers' signals the passive.

q: Your new ID cards ______ at the front desk no later than Thursday afternoon.
e: Future passive (will be + past participle): someone issues the cards; the cards do not issue anything.

q: By the end of next year, every radio in the battalion ______ with a digital model.
e: Future perfect passive (will have been + past participle) for an action completed before a future time.

q: Personal weapons ______ inside the dining facility under any circumstances.
e: Modal passive (must not be + past participle): people carry weapons, so 'weapons' takes the passive.

q: This form ______ in blue or black ink; forms completed in pencil will be returned.
e: Modal passive: should be + past participle (filled out); the form cannot fill itself out.

q: The leak in the roof ______ weeks ago; now the whole ceiling will have to be replaced.
e: Past modal passive: should have been + past participle criticizes something that was not done in the past.

q: Every soldier has the right to expect ______ fairly, regardless of rank.
e: Expect + passive infinitive (to be + past participle): the soldier receives the fair treatment.

q: Most recruits hate ______ in front of the platoon, even when they know they deserve the criticism.
e: Passive gerund (being + past participle): the recruits are singled out by someone else.

q: There ______ to be over two hundred people still trapped in the building after the earthquake.
e: Reporting passive with 'there': There are believed to be ... (= people believe there are); the verb agrees with 'people'.

q: The fire in the supply room is thought ______ by a faulty space heater.
e: Reporting passive + perfect passive infinitive: is thought to have been + past participle (an earlier event, caused by the heater).

q: Be careful with that crate of lab equipment; the glass tubes inside could easily ______ broken.
e: Get-passive after a modal: could get + past participle (= could be broken).

q: The new recruits ______ a thorough safety briefing by the range officer before the live-fire exercise.
e: Passive with two objects: the range officer gave the recruits a briefing -> the recruits were given a briefing.

q: A complaint this serious should ______ immediately by the inspector general's office.
e: The passive of a prepositional verb keeps its preposition: look into -> be looked into.

q: The equipment that ______ in Hangar 2 since Monday belongs to the engineers, not to us.
e: Present perfect passive (has been + past participle) with 'since'; someone stores the equipment.

q: The old hangar ______ next spring to make room for a longer runway.
e: 'Be going to' passive: is going to be + past participle; active 'demolish' would need an object.

q: The tires on this truck are almost bald; they need ______ before the convoy leaves.
e: Need + -ing has a passive meaning: they need replacing = they need to be replaced.

q: Most minor injuries ______ at the battalion aid station without a trip to the hospital.
e: Modal passive: can be + past participle.

q: ______ the results of the fitness test been posted on the bulletin board yet?
e: Present perfect passive question: Have + plural subject (the results) + been + past participle.

q: Do you happen to know when the original base hospital ______?
e: Indirect question: statement word order (subject + verb) with the passive 'was built'.

q: During basic training, recruits ______ the obstacle course again whenever anyone in the squad fell behind.
e: Make someone do -> passive 'be made TO do': the 'to' comes back in the passive.

q: Visitors ______ to take photographs anywhere inside the operations center.
e: 'Be allowed to' is the passive of 'allow'; 'let' is not used in the passive this way.

q: Attention, all personnel: the 1400 briefing ______ until Friday because of the power outage.
e: Present perfect passive for announcements and news: has been + past participle.

q: Before any aircraft leaves the hangar, every bolt ______ by two different mechanics.
e: Present simple passive for a routine procedure: is + past participle.

q: The new brigade commander is said ______ in three different combat zones before taking command.
e: Reporting passive about an earlier action: is said + perfect infinitive (to have served).

q: These boxes ______ left in the hallway; they're blocking the fire exit.
e: Past modal passive for criticism: shouldn't have been + past participle (someone left them there, which was wrong).

q: I can't drive you to the airport this morning; I'm ______ at the motor pool.
e: Causative: have + object + past participle (the mechanics service the truck for me).

q: Specialist Ortiz finally ______ his wisdom teeth pulled after months of pain.
e: Have + object + past participle: the dentist pulled them for him.

q: Before you deploy, you should have your will ______ by a legal assistance attorney.
e: Have + object + past participle: the attorney draws up the will for you.

q: Before the inspection, the first sergeant had the new privates ______ every window in the barracks.
e: Have + person + base form (no 'to'): he made them do the job.

q: After a week of excuses, I finally ______ the supply sergeant to issue me a new pair of boots.
e: Get + person + TO-infinitive (persuade); have, make and let take the base form without 'to'.

q: We're getting all the windows ______ before hurricane season starts.
e: Get + object + past participle: someone boards up the windows for us.

q: Sergeant Lee ______ his wallet stolen while he was on leave in Chicago.
e: Have + object + past participle can describe a bad experience: someone stole his wallet.

q: Have you ______ your eyes tested since you started getting those headaches?
e: Present perfect causative: have + had + object + past participle.

q: If the results don't improve, the company commander ______ the barracks inspected again next week.
e: Future causative: will have + object + past participle (he will arrange another inspection).

q: You should have ______ before you shipped it overseas; now nobody will pay for the damage.
e: Past causative after a modal: should have + had + object + past participle.

q: It took us all afternoon, but we finally got the old generator ______ again.
e: Get + object + -ing: make a machine start working (get the generator running).

q: ______ your teeth cleaned twice a year is fully covered by the military dental plan.
e: Gerund subject with a causative: Having + object + past participle + singular verb (is).

q: We'd better get this paperwork ______ before the commander leaves for the day.
e: Get + object + past participle: the commander signs the paperwork for us.

q: She ______ her hair dyed; it was definitely brown when I saw her last week.
e: Deduction + causative: must have had + object + past participle (I'm sure a stylist dyed it).

q: When I called, Maria was at the dealership ______ new tires put on her car.
e: Continuous causative: was having + object + past participle (mechanics were putting them on).

q: Your passport expires in May, so you'll need to ______ before your next deployment.
e: Causative with a pronoun: have + it + past participle; the object comes before the participle.

q: By the time we moved in, the landlord ______ the whole apartment repainted.
e: Past perfect causative: had + had + object + past participle (done before we moved in).

q: The lieutenant got his driver ______ him up at the airport at 0600.
e: Get + person + to-infinitive: he arranged for the driver to pick him up.

q: Captain Morales can't join us for lunch; *she's having her dress uniform altered* at the tailor shop.
o: A tailor is altering her uniform for her.
She is altering the uniform herself in the shop.
She has already finished altering her uniform.
She would like to alter it, but she can't.
e: Have + object + past participle: someone else (the tailor) does the work for her.

q: Corporal Dunn *had his laptop stolen* from his car while he was at the gym.
o: He paid someone to take his laptop.
He stole a laptop from a car.
He had already sold his laptop.
e: Have + object + past participle can describe an unpleasant event: someone stole his laptop.

q: I need to ______ this report finished by 1700, or the major will be furious.
e: Get something done = finish it, make sure it is done.

q: Last month we ______ a security system installed in our house off post.
e: Past simple causative with 'last month': had + object + past participle (a company installed it).

q: You've been on duty for eighteen hours straight; you ______ exhausted.
e: Must be: a confident deduction about the present, based on evidence.

q: Listen to all that cheering from the dayroom; our team ______.
e: Must be + -ing: deduction about something happening right now.

q: Captain Ross isn't answering his radio. I'm not sure, but he ______ in the secure briefing room, where radios must be turned off.
e: Might be: a possible (not certain) explanation for the present situation.

q: The ground is soaking wet and the trenches are full of water; it ______ hard all night.
e: Must have been + -ing: confident deduction about an activity that continued in the past.

q: Jackson ______ my email; he answered it less than five minutes after I sent it.
e: Must have + past participle: confident deduction about a past action.

q: You ______ seen Major Hill at the gym this morning; he's been in Germany since Monday.
e: Can't have + past participle: I'm sure it did not happen (it was impossible).

q: All the glass from the broken window is outside the house, so the burglar ______ that way.
e: Can't have + past participle (broken, not broke): a logical conclusion that something did not happen.

q: Sorry I missed your call last night; I ______ in the shower.
e: Must have been: deduction about where someone (even the speaker) was at a past time.

q: I'm not sure where my ID card is. I ______ it in the copier on the second floor.
e: Might have + past participle: a possibility about the past.

q: That was a dangerous turn, Private! You ______ the truck over!
e: Could have + past participle: something was possible in the past but did not happen.

q: The documents ______ extremely sensitive, or the courier wouldn't have needed an armed escort.
e: Must have been: deduction from evidence (the armed escort).

q: Chen looks completely worn out. He ______ all night for the promotion board.
e: May have been + -ing: a possible explanation involving a continuous past activity.

q: Who ______ the armory door unlocked? It was wide open when I arrived at 0500.
e: Could have + past participle in questions about possible explanations for the past.

q: Jim ______ hungry already; he ate two cheeseburgers less than an hour ago!
e: Can't be: a present deduction that something is impossible.

q: The package was mailed on Monday, so it ______ here by Thursday at the latest.
e: Should be: what we logically expect to be true (expectation, not obligation).

q: The convoy left at noon. It ______ by now, so why haven't we heard from them?
e: Should have + past participle: something we expected to have happened by now.

q: The report isn't on the shared drive. It ______ by mistake during last night's system update.
e: Passive deduction about the past: may have been + past participle.

q: Private Kowalski ______ in the swamp all morning; his uniform is spotless.
e: Can't have been + -ing: I'm sure the activity was not happening (the evidence shows the opposite).

q: We ______ the mission without the local guides; they knew every trail in those mountains.
e: Couldn't have + past participle: it would have been impossible (without the guides we would have failed).

q: Rodriguez *can't have forgotten* about the drill; I reminded him twice this morning.
e: Can't have + past participle = I'm sure it didn't happen.

q: Where's the general? His flight *must have been delayed* again.
o: I'm almost sure the flight was delayed.
Someone ordered the flight to be delayed.
The flight will probably be delayed.
Perhaps the flight was delayed, but I doubt it.
e: Must have been + past participle: a confident deduction about a past event (passive).

q: You *could have been* seriously hurt jumping off that wall!
o: It was possible, but it didn't happen.
You were allowed to get hurt.
You were seriously hurt, as I had predicted.
e: Could have been + past participle: something was possible in the past but did not happen.

q: Your Spanish is excellent! You ______ in Latin America for years.
e: Must have + past participle: a confident deduction from evidence (your excellent Spanish).

q: Don't worry if Tanaka hasn't replied yet; he ______ your message.
e: May not have + past participle (seen): perhaps something did not happen.

q: It ______ easy for your parents when they moved to a new country with three small children.
e: Can't have been: a past deduction (I'm sure it wasn't easy) about a past time ('when they moved').

q: Everyone showed up at 0500 instead of 0600, so they ______ the wrong time.
e: Passive deduction: must have been + past participle (someone told them the wrong time).

q: We ______ so much water; there was a fresh supply waiting for us at the checkpoint.
e: Needn't have + past participle: we did it, but it turned out to be unnecessary.

q: Saturday's formation was canceled, so we ______ get up at 0500 for once.
e: Didn't have to + base form: there was no obligation in the past.

q: Thanks, but you *needn't have brought* your own sleeping bag; the barracks has plenty of bedding.
o: You brought it, but it wasn't necessary.
You didn't bring it, and that was the right choice.
You weren't allowed to bring it.
You should have brought a better one.
e: Needn't have + past participle: the action happened, but it was not necessary.

q: Civilian contractors ______ wear a uniform on base, but they ______ forget to display their ID badges.
o: don't have to / don't need to
e: Don't have to = it is not necessary; must not = it is forbidden.

q: The briefing was a disaster. You ______ the slides before presenting them to the general.
e: Should have + past participle: criticism of something that was not done.

q: I ______ that third cup of coffee; now I can't fall asleep.
e: Shouldn't have + past participle (drunk, not drank): regret about a past action.

q: The patrol ______ reported back by 2200, but nobody has heard from them yet.
e: Ought to have + past participle: something expected or required did not happen.

q: The new printer ______ arrive last Tuesday, but it still hasn't been delivered.
e: Was supposed to: something planned or expected in the past that did not happen.

q: According to the order, all personnel ______ report to Hangar 4 at 0700 tomorrow in full gear.
e: Be + to-infinitive: a formal instruction or official arrangement (= must).

q: You ______ tell the first sergeant about the accident before he hears about it from someone else.
e: Had better + base form (no 'to'): strong advice with a warning.

q: The bridge had been washed out, so the convoy ______ take a 40-mile detour.
e: Had to: past obligation; 'must' has no past form, and 'must have' expresses deduction.

q: If the weather doesn't improve by noon, the parachute jump ______.
e: Future obligation + passive: will have to be + past participle ('will' cannot be followed by 'must').

q: The guard recognized me, so I ______ my ID; in fact, I never even took it out of my wallet.
e: Didn't need to: it wasn't necessary, so I didn't do it; 'needn't have shown' would mean I showed it anyway.

q: You ______ during the safety briefing instead of texting your girlfriend!
e: Should have been + -ing: criticism of what someone was (not) doing at a past time.

q: Do officers ______ attend the change-of-command ceremony, or is it optional for them?
e: After 'do' in a question, use 'have to' (Do ... have to ...?); must, need and ought do not fit here.

q: The doctor told me that I ______ stay off my feet for at least a week after the surgery.
e: In reported speech, must / have to usually becomes 'had to'.

q: All visitors ______ to show a valid photo ID at the main gate.
e: Passive of 'require': be required to (= must).

q: Cell phones ______ into the secure area under any circumstances; leave them in the lockers outside.
e: Must not + passive: a prohibition (it is forbidden), not a lack of necessity.

q: You ______ meet me at the airport; I can easily catch a cab to the base.
e: Needn't + base form: it is not necessary (now or in the future).

q: Starting next year, all pilots ______ pass a new simulator test before they are cleared to fly.
e: Future obligation: will have to (there is no 'will must').

q: You ______ asked me for a ride; I was driving right past your building anyway.
e: Could have + past participle: an option that existed but was not used.

q: The supply clerk ______ issued the night-vision goggles without a signed hand receipt.
e: Ought not to have + past participle: criticism of a past action (= shouldn't have).

q: In my old unit, we ______ leave the base without a pass; it was strictly forbidden.
e: Past prohibition: weren't allowed to ('must not' has no past form; 'didn't have to' = no obligation).

q: I've ______ finish this report tonight; it's due on the colonel's desk at 0800.
e: Have got to (common in informal American English) = have to: a strong present obligation.
