q: This morning Sergeant Diaz said he ______ going to finish the inventory before lunch, but it's now 1400 and he hasn't even started.
e: After a past reporting verb, 'am going to' moves back to 'was going to'; the plan is no longer current.

q: On Monday the supply clerk told me the new boots ______ by Friday, but Friday came and went with no delivery.
e: 'Will' in the original words becomes 'would' (future in the past) when the time has already passed.

q: When we got back to the gas station, the driver was gone, even though he had promised he would wait ______ until we returned.
e: In reported speech 'here' becomes 'there' when the reporter is no longer in that place.

q: The duty officer ______ us that the main gate would close at 2200 sharp.
e: 'Tell' takes the listener directly (told us); 'say', 'explain' and 'announce' need 'to us'.

q: The recruiter ______ to me that the enlistment bonus had been cut in half.
e: 'Mention to someone that...' is correct; 'tell', 'inform' and 'notify' take the person directly, without 'to'.

q: The first sergeant told us, "You must sign out before you leave post." In other words, he told us we ______ sign out before we left post.
e: Reported obligation: 'must' usually becomes 'had to'; 'must to' and 'had must' do not exist.

q: When I met him in 2015, Tom told me he ______ speak three languages, but he has forgotten most of his French since then.
e: 'Can' becomes 'could' after a past reporting verb, especially when the fact is no longer true.

q: The witness told the MPs that she ______ the car somewhere before, but she couldn't remember where.
e: An experience earlier than the past moment of speaking is reported with the past perfect: 'had seen'.

q: Private Lopez said, "I've been waiting here for over an hour!" Later he complained to the sergeant that he ______ there for over an hour.
e: Present perfect continuous ('have been waiting') moves back to past perfect continuous ('had been waiting').

q: Our physics instructor reminded us that sound ______ faster through water than through air.
e: A scientific fact that is always true usually keeps the present simple in reported speech.

q: Last month Lee said to me, "I'll call you tomorrow." So Lee told me he would call me ______, but he never did.
e: When reported later, 'tomorrow' becomes 'the next day' (or 'the following day').

q: The sergeant just called from the motor pool; he says he ______ us at the east gate in about ten minutes.
e: With a present reporting verb ('says'), the tense of the original words does not change: 'will meet'.

q: When I called the clinic last month, the nurse said my lab results ______ ready until the following week, but they actually took three weeks.
e: Past reporting: 'won't be ... next week' becomes 'wouldn't be ... the following week'.

q: The pharmacist warned me ______ this medication with alcohol.
e: warn + person + (not) to-infinitive: warned me not to take.

q: At the end of the briefing, the colonel suggested ______ the exercise until the weather improved.
e: suggest + -ing (or suggest that we postpone); 'suggest someone to do' is wrong.

q: Under questioning, the private finally admitted ______ the keys to the supply room.
e: admit + -ing / having + past participle; 'admit' is never followed by a to-infinitive.

q: "No way. I am not signing anything," the contractor said. In other words, the contractor ______ to sign the papers.
e: refuse + to-infinitive; 'deny' takes -ing, 'reject' takes a noun, and 'object to' takes -ing.

q: The nurse asked me ______ my sleeve so she could take my blood pressure.
e: A reported request: ask + person + to-infinitive.

q: "Would you mind not smoking in the truck?" the driver asked. So the driver asked me ______ in the truck.
o: if I mind not to smoke
e: A polite request is reported as ask + person + (not) to-infinitive: asked me not to smoke.

q: The landlord threatened ______ the police if we didn't turn the music down.
e: threaten + to-infinitive, with no person object before it.

q: Could you explain ______ how the new travel pay system works?
e: explain something to someone; 'explain me' is a very common error.

q: The recruiter asked me ______ any tattoos or body piercings.
e: Reported yes/no question: if/whether + subject + verb (statement order), with backshift.

q: My platoon leader asked me where ______ the night before, since I had missed bed check.
e: Reported wh-question: statement word order plus backshift: where I had been.

q: The customs officer wanted to know how long ______ in the country.
e: In a reported question there is no 'did' and no inversion: how long I planned to stay.

q: We couldn't decide ______ to drive or fly to my cousin's wedding in Texas.
e: Only 'whether' (not 'if') can come directly before a to-infinitive: whether to drive or fly.

q: There was a long discussion at the staff meeting about ______ the base should hire more civilian mechanics.
e: After a preposition (about), use 'whether', not 'if'.

q: The MP asked who ______ the vehicle when the accident happened.
e: When 'who' is the subject, the verb follows it directly: who was driving.

q: "Can you work this Saturday?" my supervisor asked. In other words, my supervisor asked ______ work that Saturday.
e: A yes/no question is reported with if/whether; 'can' becomes 'could'; statement order.

q: The clerk asked, "Shall I close the window?" In other words, the clerk asked if she ______ close the window.
e: An offer with 'Shall I...?' is reported with 'should': asked if she should close it.

q: My mother kept asking me what the food at basic training ______.
e: 'What was it like?' becomes 'what the food was like' (subject before verb).

q: The commander wanted to know why the generator ______ been serviced on schedule.
e: Reported question: why + subject + verb, with past perfect for the earlier failure: why it hadn't been serviced.

q: A tourist stopped me outside the train station and asked where she ______ a bus to the airport.
e: Reported question: where + subject + verb, no inversion; the subject 'she' is already there.

q: Every night the kids asked when Dad ______ home from his deployment.
e: Reported question about the future in the past: when Dad would come (no inversion).

q: On his first night in the barracks, the new private asked the sergeant what ______ if the fire alarm went off.
e: A question word + to-infinitive can replace a reported question: what to do.

q: Excuse me, could you tell me where ______? I have an appointment at 0930.
e: Indirect question: question word + subject + verb: where the dental clinic is.

q: Do you have any idea what time ______ on weekends?
e: After 'Do you have any idea...', use statement order without 'does': what time it opens.

q: I'm not sure ______ to complete this course, so I'll ask the education office.
o: how many credits do I need
e: Indirect question: how many + plural noun + subject + verb, no 'do'.

q: Can you remember ______ the spare key to the Humvee? We need it before 0700.
e: Indirect question: where + subject + verb, with no auxiliary 'did'.

q: What do you think ______ to the meeting tomorrow? He never comes empty-handed.
e: After 'What do you think...?', the rest of the question has statement order: what do you think he will bring?

q: Does anyone know who ______ the light on in the arms room last night?
e: 'Who' is the subject here, so the verb follows directly, with no auxiliary: who left.

q: I wonder ______ so quiet today; he usually never stops talking.
e: After 'I wonder', use statement order: why the sergeant is so quiet.

q: Could you tell me ______ the briefing will last? I have a dental appointment at ten.
e: 'How long' asks about duration; in an indirect question it is followed by subject + verb.

q: The manual doesn't say ______ the air filter should be replaced.
e: 'How often' asks about frequency; the indirect question keeps statement order (the filter should be...).

q: Nobody told us ______ to the range, so we had to find a ride on our own.
e: Indirect question after a past verb: how + subject + verb, no inversion and no 'did'.

q: Let me check ______ any seats left on the 0600 flight to Atlanta.
e: Indirect yes/no question: whether + there + verb; 'seats' is plural, so 'there are'.

q: Do you know ______ the PX is open on Sundays?
e: An embedded yes/no question starts with 'if' or 'whether'.

q: The real question is ______ enough fuel to reach the next airfield.
e: An embedded question after 'The question is' keeps statement order: whether we have.

q: Nobody can say yet ______ the damage to the hangar is.
e: 'How' + adjective (not adverb) before the subject: how serious the damage is.

q: He keeps mentioning some new regulation, but honestly, I have no idea ______.
e: Indirect question with statement order; the preposition stays at the end: what he's talking about.

q: Tell me ______ you're so upset about, and maybe I can help.
e: Embedded 'What is it (that) you're upset about?' takes statement order: what it is you're upset about.

q: Can anyone tell me ______? It was left on the firing line after qualification.
o: who does this rifle belong to
e: Indirect question: who + subject + verb + preposition, with no 'does'.

q: We need to find out ______ the old bridge can hold before we send the trucks across.
e: 'Weight' is uncountable (how much), and the indirect question keeps statement order.

q: Who do you think ______ the championship this year?
e: 'Who' is the subject of 'win', so after 'do you think' the verb follows directly: who do you think will win?

q: Who did you say ______ the new supply sergeant? I didn't catch his name.
e: 'Who' is the subject of 'was': Who did you say was the new supply sergeant? No extra pronoun.

q: I'm curious ______ he managed to pass the PT test with a knee injury.
e: Indirect question: how + subject + verb, with no 'did'.

q: I can't recall ______ at the reunion last summer; there were so many people.
e: Indirect question: who + subject + verb + preposition at the end, no 'did'.

q: I'm not the only one who failed the uniform inspection, ______?
e: A negative statement takes a positive tag: I'm not..., am I?

q: Let's take a ten-minute break before the next block of instruction, ______?
e: A suggestion with 'Let's' takes the tag 'shall we?'.

q: Hand me that torque wrench, ______?
e: After an imperative, the tag is will/would/can/could you.

q: Don't forget to sign out at the front desk before you leave, ______?
e: A negative imperative takes the tag 'will you?'.

q: No one ever tells us anything around here, ______?
e: 'No one' makes the sentence negative, so the tag is positive and uses 'they': do they?

q: There's a safety briefing at 1500 today, ______?
e: 'There is' keeps 'there' in the tag: isn't there?

q: Everyone passed the land navigation course, ______?
e: everyone / everybody becomes 'they' in the tag: didn't they?

q: He hardly ever complains about the long hours, ______?
e: 'Hardly ever' is negative in meaning, so the tag is positive: does he?

q: You'd better report this to the duty officer right away, ______?
e: 'You'd better' = you had better, so the tag is 'hadn't you?'.

q: You'd rather stay on base this weekend than drive to the city, ______?
e: 'You'd rather' = you would rather, so the tag is 'wouldn't you?'.

q: She used to be stationed in Germany, ______?
e: 'Used to' forms its tag with 'did': didn't she?

q: We have to turn in our cold-weather gear by Friday, ______?
e: 'Have to' behaves like a main verb, so the tag uses 'do': don't we?

q: Your brother has a new pickup truck, ______?
e: In American English, 'have' meaning possess takes 'do' in the tag: doesn't he?

q: Nothing was damaged in last night's storm, ______?
e: 'Nothing' is negative and is replaced by 'it': was it?

q: I don't think the bus will be on time today, ______?
e: After 'I don't think', the tag matches the second clause and is positive: will it?

q: Few people knew about the change in the training schedule, ______?
e: 'Few' (not 'a few') is negative in meaning, so the tag is positive: did they?

q: The captain's never been to Alaska, ______?
e: Here 's = has (been), and 'never' is negative, so the tag is 'has he?'.

q: He'd already left by the time you got there, ______?
e: 'He'd left' = he had left (past participle), so the tag is 'hadn't he?'.

q: She'd never miss a formation without calling first, ______?
e: 'She'd' + base verb = she would; with 'never' the tag is positive: would she?

q: Your unit's been here since March, ______?
e: 'Unit's been' = unit has been, so the tag is 'hasn't it?'.

q: You couldn't give me a ride to the motor pool, ______?
e: A polite negative request takes a positive tag with the same auxiliary: could you?

q: Those are the new armor plates we ordered, ______?
e: 'These' and 'those' become 'they' in tag questions.

q: Who ______ you to the hospital after the accident?
e: When 'who' is the subject, there is no 'did': Who drove you?

q: Who ______ for directions when you got lost downtown?
e: Object question: question word + did + subject + base verb: Who did you ask?

q: What ______ to the old radar station after the Air Force closed it?
e: 'What' is the subject, so no 'did'; 'happen' has no passive.

q: What's this tool ______? I've never seen one like it.
e: 'What is it for?' asks about purpose.

q: ______ did you travel with on your last leave?
e: The preposition stays at the end (Who ... with?); it cannot appear twice.

q: How come you ______ me about the schedule change?
e: 'How come' is followed by statement word order (no inversion): How come you didn't tell me?

q: What's the new lieutenant ______? Is she easy to work for?
e: 'What is someone like?' asks about a person's character.

q: A: "Didn't you lock the arms room?" B: "______. I checked it twice before I left."
e: Answer the facts, not the form of the question: if you locked it, say 'Yes, I did', even after a negative question.

q: A: "Kim got promoted to staff sergeant last week." B: "______? Good for her!"
e: A reply question repeats the auxiliary of the statement; past simple 'got' takes 'Did she?'.

q: ______ are these? Somebody left them in the dayroom.
e: 'Whose' + noun asks about the owner; 'who's' means 'who is'.

q: How long ______ for your security clearance to come through?
e: 'How long' + present perfect continuous for a wait that started in the past and continues now; auxiliary before subject.

q: Why ______ the ceremony moved indoors at the last minute?
e: Passive question: Why + was + subject + past participle ('moved' is a participle here).

q: ______ to get your shots before you deploy?
e: Negative question: auxiliary + n't + subject + base verb: Don't you need...?

q: What ______ you do if your vehicle broke down in the middle of the desert?
e: A hypothetical question with a past-tense if-clause uses 'would': What would you do if...?

q: ______ was at the meeting besides the commander?
e: 'Else' follows the question word; 'who' (not 'whom') is the subject of 'was'.

q: Who ______ the coffee machine? It's not working again.
e: Subject question with 'who': singular verb and the past participle 'broken'.

q: ______ packed yet? We move out in an hour!
e: 'Packed' is a past participle here, so the question needs the present perfect: Haven't you packed yet?

q: Why ______ the train instead of driving all that way by yourself?
e: 'Why not' + base verb makes a suggestion: Why not take the train?

q: ______ anyone here who speaks Tagalog? We need an interpreter.
e: 'Anyone' is singular, and a question inverts 'there is': Is there anyone...?

q: What did the doctor ______ about your knee?
e: After 'did' use the base form; 'say' needs no person object, while 'tell' does (tell you).

q: Why ______ the alarm when you first saw the smoke?
e: Negative wh-question: Why + didn't + subject + base verb.

q: ______ responsible for locking up the arms room tonight?
e: 'Who's' = who is; the sentence needs a verb before 'responsible'.

q: On the drive back from Fort Hood, we stopped ______ lunch at a small diner outside Waco.
e: stop + to-infinitive = stop in order to do something; stop + -ing = no longer do it.

q: My knee finally stopped ______ after six weeks of physical therapy, so I'm running again.
e: stop + -ing = an action or state ends. 'Stopped to hurt' would mean 'stopped in order to hurt'.

q: I clearly remember ______ the arms room door before I left, so someone else must have opened it.
e: remember + -ing looks back at a past action; remember + to-infinitive means not forgetting a task.

q: Please remember ______ your ID card when you report to the armory tomorrow morning.
e: remember + to-infinitive = do not forget a future task.

q: I'll never forget ______ the coastline through the open door of the C-130 on my very first jump.
e: never forget + -ing = always keep the memory of a past experience.

q: The generator ran out of fuel overnight because someone had forgotten ______ it after the evening shift.
e: forget + to-infinitive = fail to do something you should have done.

q: We regret ______ you that your request for a transfer to Fort Carson has not been approved.
e: regret + to-infinitive announces bad news politely: 'We regret to inform you...'.

q: Corporal Diaz now regrets ______ his entire reenlistment bonus on a sports car he can't afford to insure.
e: regret + -ing = be sorry about something you did in the past.

q: If your phone won't connect to the base Wi-Fi, try ______ it off and on again; that usually solves the problem.
e: try + -ing = do something as an experiment to see whether it works.

q: The lieutenant tried her best ______ calm when the radio reported enemy contact.
e: try (one's best) + to-infinitive = make an effort to do something difficult.

q: On the way to the range, the driver *stopped to check* the tire pressure.
o: He paused in order to check it.
He gave up checking it regularly.
He no longer bothered to check it.
He checked it without slowing down.
e: stop + to-infinitive = interrupt one activity in order to do another.

q: The radio was dead, so I *tried changing* the batteries, but it still didn't work.
o: I changed them to see if that would help.
I wanted to change them but was unable to.
I refused to change them a second time.
I forgot to change them before leaving.
e: try + -ing = do something as an experiment; here the batteries really were changed.

q: She says she *doesn't remember signing* the hand receipt for the night-vision goggles.
o: She can't recall having signed it.
She forgot that she had to sign it.
She does not want to sign it again.
She will not forget to sign it.
e: remember + -ing = have a memory of a past action; she may have signed it but cannot recall doing so.

q: After the inspection, the sergeant *went on to explain* the new leave policy.
o: Next, he moved on and explained it.
He kept explaining it for a long time.
He refused to explain it any further.
He explained it before the inspection.
e: go on + to-infinitive = do something new next; go on + -ing = continue the same action.

q: Accepting the overseas assignment would mean ______ away from my wife and kids for at least a year.
e: mean + -ing = involve or result in; mean + to-infinitive = intend.

q: Sorry, I meant ______ you back last night, but the phone lines on the base were down.
e: mean + to-infinitive = intend to do something.

q: The instructor asked for silence twice, but the two recruits in the back row just went on ______.
e: go on + -ing = continue doing the same thing; go on + to-infinitive = move on to something new.

q: The windshield wipers on this Humvee are badly worn; they need ______ before the rainy season starts.
e: need + -ing has a passive meaning: they need replacing = they need to be replaced.

q: Would you like ______ the base museum while you're here at Fort Sill?
e: would like is followed by the to-infinitive.

q: I remember ______ the letter, but I forgot ______ a stamp on it, so it came back to me a week later.
e: remember + -ing = a memory of a past action; forget + to-infinitive = fail to do a necessary task.

q: Stop ______ about the chow hall food, and remember ______ the cooks before you leave.
e: stop + -ing = quit an action; remember + to-infinitive = don't forget a task still to be done.

q: I *regret to say* that tomorrow's live-fire exercise has been canceled because of high winds.
o: I am sorry that I have to tell you
I am sorry that I told you earlier
I am happy to be able to tell you
I am not allowed to tell you
e: regret + to-infinitive = be sorry about the news you are about to give.

q: I'll *never forget meeting* the Sergeant Major of the Army at my graduation.
o: I must be sure to do it.
I will never do it again.
I have no memory of it.
e: never forget + -ing = always keep the memory of a past event.

q: The suspect denied ______ anywhere near the motor pool on the night of the break-in.
e: deny is followed by -ing (or having + past participle), never by the to-infinitive.

q: Have you ever considered ______ for the warrant officer program? You'd be a strong candidate.
e: consider is followed by the -ing form.

q: With his evaluation coming up next month, the new lieutenant can't afford ______ another mistake.
e: afford is followed by the to-infinitive: can't afford to do something.

q: Every time Sergeant Hall tells that story about the lost goat, I can't help ______.
e: can't help + -ing = be unable to stop yourself from doing something.

q: It's not worth ______ the dispatcher now; she went off duty an hour ago.
e: be worth is followed by the -ing form.

q: After three hours of digging, the squad finally managed ______ the truck out of the mud.
e: manage + to-infinitive = succeed in doing something difficult.

q: The driver pretended ______ the sentry's signal and drove straight through the checkpoint.
e: pretend is followed by the to-infinitive; the negative is 'pretend not to do'.

q: Most recruits hate ______ at by the drill sergeants, but they soon learn to ignore it.
e: Passive gerund: hate + being + past participle (the recruits are the ones yelled at).

q: All visitors should expect ______ at the main gate, so please have your ID ready.
e: Passive infinitive: expect + to be + past participle (the visitors are searched).

q: Judging by the broken latch, the thieves seem ______ in through the back window last night.
e: seem + perfect infinitive (to have + past participle) refers to an earlier, finished action.

q: ______ the safety briefing twice, the crew knew exactly what to do when the engine caught fire.
e: Having + past participle shows an action completed before the main action.

q: Our battalion is committed to ______ the response time for medical emergencies by half.
e: In 'be committed to', 'to' is a preposition, so it is followed by the -ing form.

q: Many of the reservists objected to ______ on weekends without being paid for it.
e: object to + -ing: here 'to' is a preposition, not part of an infinitive.

q: Instead of ______ the problem to his chain of command, the specialist tried to fix it himself.
e: After a preposition such as 'instead of', use the -ing form.

q: The heavy rain prevented the helicopters ______ on schedule.
e: prevent someone/something from + -ing.

q: The first sergeant accused two privates ______ the vending machine in the dayroom.
e: accuse someone of + -ing.

q: The doctor advised Sergeant Kim ______ anything heavier than ten pounds for six weeks.
e: advise + object + (not) to-infinitive.

q: The colonel wants all section chiefs ______ their training reports by Thursday noon.
e: want + object + to-infinitive; 'want that someone...' is not used in English.

q: The flight surgeon made the pilot ______ on the ground for 48 hours because of an ear infection.
e: make + object + bare infinitive (no 'to') in the active voice.

q: After failing the inspection, the entire platoon was made ______ the barracks all over again.
e: In the passive, make takes the to-infinitive: be made to do something.

q: The gate guard let us ______ without even checking the trunk.
e: let + object + bare infinitive.

q: I'd rather ______ out at the base gym for free than pay forty dollars a month in town.
e: would rather + bare infinitive.

q: The medic suggested ______ the hiker some water and keeping him in the shade until the ambulance arrived.
e: suggest + -ing (or suggest that we give); 'suggest someone to do' is wrong.

q: For desert conditions, the technical manual recommends ______ the air filter every 3,000 miles.
e: recommend + -ing (or recommend that someone do); not 'recommend to do'.

q: Could you remind me ______ the updated training schedule to the new arrivals this afternoon?
e: remind + object + to-infinitive = make someone remember a task.

q: The new tracking system enables commanders ______ the location of every vehicle in real time.
e: enable + object + to-infinitive.

q: Sergeant Major Owens insisted on ______ every vehicle himself before the convoy left the gate.
e: insist on + -ing (insist is followed by the preposition 'on').

q: After eight months in the field, the troops were really looking forward to ______ a long hot shower.
e: look forward to + -ing: 'to' is a preposition here.

q: Specialist Lee went to the education center ______ about tuition assistance for night classes.
e: Use the to-infinitive to express a person's purpose, not 'for + -ing'.

q: Private Moore isn't strong ______ the 60-pound rucksack for the whole twelve-mile march yet.
e: adjective + enough + to-infinitive: strong enough to carry.

q: It took the engineers almost three days ______ the bridge after the flood.
e: It takes (someone) + time + to-infinitive.

q: The battalion spent the whole afternoon ______ for the general's visit.
e: spend + time + -ing.

q: Many soldiers newly assigned to Fort Carson have trouble ______ to the high altitude.
e: have trouble (or difficulty) + -ing.

q: Staff Sergeant Reyes was the first woman in her unit ______ the Sapper Leader Course.
e: After 'the first / the last / the only + noun', use the to-infinitive: the first woman to complete.

q: Nobody told the new clerk ______ the classified documents at the end of the day.
e: tell + object + question word + to-infinitive: where to store, how to do, what to say.

q: Volunteers from the battalion helped the flood victims ______ their damaged homes.
e: help + object + bare infinitive (or to-infinitive): help someone (to) clean up.

q: Two men were seen ______ the warehouse just before the fire alarm went off.
e: In the passive, verbs of perception take -ing or the to-infinitive: were seen leaving / were seen to leave.

q: Despite the heat, the medics kept ______ until every casualty had been treated.
e: keep (on) + -ing = continue doing something.

q: After the heavy rain, nobody wanted to risk ______ the river in the old trucks.
e: risk is followed by the -ing form.

q: The commander decided to postpone ______ the new duty roster until after the holidays.
e: postpone (delay, put off) + -ing.

q: The private refused ______ the order because he believed it was unsafe.
e: refuse is followed by the to-infinitive.

q: After a long silence, the private finally admitted ______ the keys in the ignition.
e: admit + -ing (or admit to + -ing).

q: Since moving to Arizona, I really miss ______ in the ocean on weekends.
e: miss + -ing = feel sad that you no longer do something.

q: The pilot ______ helicopter went down near the border was rescued after two days in the mountains.
e: whose shows possession (the pilot's helicopter); who's = who is.

q: The base ______ my father worked in the 1980s has since been turned into a state park.
e: Use where for a place when the clause is complete (he worked there); 'which' would need 'in' or 'at'.

q: This is the training area ______ we visited during our first week of orientation.
e: 'visited' needs an object, so use that/which (object pronoun), not where.

q: I'll never forget the cold morning ______ we got the order to deploy.
e: when introduces a relative clause after a time noun (= on which).

q: The year ______ followed my deployment was the hardest of my whole career.
e: The pronoun is the subject of 'followed', so use that/which, not when.

q: My roommate, ______ is a combat medic, showed me how to apply a tourniquet properly.
e: Non-defining clauses (between commas) use who/which, never that.

q: Sergeant Blake failed the swim test for the third time, ______ surprised everyone in the company.
e: which can refer to a whole previous clause; that and what cannot be used this way.

q: The officer to ______ you should address your leave request is Captain Ruiz.
e: After a preposition, use whom for people (which for things); never 'that'.

q: The new recruits, most of ______ had never been away from home before, were nervous on the first night.
e: quantifier + of + whom (people) in a non-defining clause: most of whom.

q: The trucks, several of ______ were more than twenty years old, were finally replaced last spring.
e: quantifier + of + which (things) in a non-defining clause: several of which.

q: Lieutenant Price is the officer ______ I think will be promoted first.
e: who is the subject of 'will be promoted'; 'I think' is only inserted, so whom is wrong.

q: The unit in ______ my brother serves is stationed in Germany.
e: After a preposition, use which for things; 'in that' and 'in where' are wrong.

q: Can you give me one good reason ______ we should change the plan this late?
e: the reason why + clause.

q: The dental clinic ______ hours were extended last month now stays open until 9 p.m. on weekdays.
e: whose can refer to things as well as people: the clinic's hours.

q: Everything ______ the instructor said during the safety briefing was recorded on video.
e: After everything, all or nothing, use that (or no pronoun), not what.

q: ______ the instructor told us during the safety briefing turned out to be very useful.
e: What = the thing(s) that; the what-clause is the subject of the sentence.

q: Soldiers ______ in the training accident were flown to the hospital at Landstuhl.
e: Reduced relative clause: injured = who were injured (passive meaning).

q: Anyone ______ to join the trip to the Grand Canyon should sign up at the MWR office by Friday.
e: Reduced relative clause: wishing = who wishes; 'anyone who wish' is wrong because anyone is singular.

q: Those of you ______ have not turned in your medical forms must do so by Friday.
e: who is the subject of the relative clause and refers to people.

q: The convoy reached the river at 1800, by ______ time the bridge had already been destroyed.
e: by which time = and by that time; which can follow a preposition and refer back to a time.

q: The morning flight may be canceled because of fog, in ______ case we will drive to the conference instead.
e: in which case = and if that happens.

q: This is the only map ______ shows the old logging roads in the area.
e: that refers to a thing and is the subject of 'shows'.

q: The briefing room, ______ seats about 200 people, is closed for renovation until March.
e: Non-defining clause about a thing: which (not that); where cannot be the subject of 'seats'.

q: The sergeant ______ is on leave until the end of the month.
o: with whom I usually work with
e: The object pronoun can be left out (I usually work with); never repeat the preposition or add 'him'.

q: The laptop ______ at the PX last week has already stopped working.
e: Do not add an object pronoun (it) inside the relative clause; 'what' cannot follow a noun.

q: Dr. Patel, ______ many of you met at the clinic, will lead tomorrow's first-aid class.
e: whom is the object of 'met'; that cannot be used in a non-defining clause.

q: Our unit was first deployed in 2019, ______ I was still in high school.
e: when in a non-defining clause after a time expression (= and at that time).

q: The new radios are exactly ______ we needed for operations in the mountains.
e: what = the thing that; no noun comes before it.

q: Joining the Army was the best decision ______ I have ever made.
e: After a superlative + noun, use that; what cannot follow a noun.

q: The equipment ______ in this week's exercise belongs to the National Guard.
e: Reduced relative clause in the passive progressive: being used = which is being used.

q: The building, the roof ______ was damaged in the storm, will be torn down next year.
e: the roof of which = whose roof (a formal pattern for things).

q: The old barracks ______ had no air conditioning, so summers were miserable.
e: Say '(that) we lived in', 'in which we lived' or 'where we lived'; never use the preposition twice.

q: Friday is the day ______ the new duty schedule takes effect.
e: Days take 'on', so the relative form is 'on which' (= when).

q: After the accident, Specialist Grant badly needed someone ______ to.
e: noun + to-infinitive (+ preposition): someone to talk to.

q: Sergeant Ortiz was ______ first soldier in her company to qualify as ______ expert marksman.
e: Ordinal numbers take 'the' (the first soldier); 'expert' begins with a vowel sound, so we say 'an expert'.

q: A car alarm went off at 3 a.m. for the third night in a row, so one of the neighbors finally called ______ police.
e: 'The police' is a group noun that always takes 'the': call the police.

q: The new recruit wore ______ uniform that was two sizes too big and carried ______ M4 that had seen better days.
e: Choose a/an by sound: 'uniform' starts with a /j/ (you) sound, so 'a uniform'; 'M4' starts with the vowel sound /em/, so 'an M4'.

q: ______ injured were flown to the medical center at Landstuhl within an hour of the explosion.
e: 'The + adjective' names a whole group of people (the injured, the wounded, the elderly) and takes a plural verb.

q: ______ more you practice your reloading drills, the faster you will be when it really counts.
e: Double comparative: 'The more ..., the faster ...' needs 'the' in both parts.

q: ______ number of soldiers applying for the airborne course has doubled since last year.
e: 'The number of + plural noun' takes a singular verb (has doubled). 'A number of' means 'several' and takes a plural verb.

q: Last summer the recruits hiked through ______ Rocky Mountains and then climbed ______ Pikes Peak.
e: Mountain ranges take 'the' (the Rocky Mountains), but single mountains and peaks take no article (Pikes Peak, Mount Rainier).

q: Lieutenant Brooks speaks ______ Arabic fluently because she spent most of her childhood in ______ Middle East.
e: Languages take no article (speak Arabic); some regions always take 'the': the Middle East, the Midwest.

q: We're having a barbecue with ______ Johnsons, our new neighbors from across the street, on Saturday.
e: A family name in the plural takes 'the': the Johnsons = the Johnson family.

q: During cold weather, the generator has to be checked at least twice ______ day.
e: Frequency is expressed with a/an: twice a day, once a week, three times a month.

q: Captain Reyes is ______ only officer in the battalion who has served in both Korea and Kosovo.
e: 'Only' makes the noun unique, so it takes 'the': the only officer.

q: We usually have ______ lunch at noon, but ______ lunch they served at the field kitchen today came two hours late.
e: Meals in general take no article (have lunch); a specific, identified meal takes 'the' (the lunch they served).

q: Is there ______ European officer on the panel, or are all the members from Asia and Africa?
e: 'European' begins with a /j/ (you) sound, so it takes 'a', not 'an'.

q: What ______ terrible weather we had during last week's field exercise!
e: 'Weather' is uncountable, so the exclamation is 'What + adjective + uncountable noun' with no article.

q: Before I moved off post, my first sergeant gave me ______ about finding a good apartment.
e: 'Advice' is uncountable: no a/an and no plural. Use 'some advice' or 'a piece of advice'.

q: The ship sailed through ______ Panama Canal on its way to its new home port in ______ San Diego.
e: Canals, rivers and oceans take 'the' (the Panama Canal); most cities take no article (San Diego).

q: I bought ______ one-way ticket to Seattle and ______ used car as soon as I got there.
e: Choose by sound: 'one' starts with a /w/ sound and 'used' with a /j/ sound, so both take 'a'.

q: Sergeant Kim is ______ honorable man; he would never lie in ______ official report.
e: 'Honorable' has a silent h and 'official' starts with a vowel sound, so both take 'an'.

q: That was by far ______ hardest ruck march I've ever done, and I've done dozens of them.
e: Superlatives take 'the': the hardest, the best, the most difficult.

q: My sister went to ______ University of Michigan, and my brother studied at ______ Boston University.
e: 'The University of + place' takes 'the'; 'Place + University' takes no article (Boston University).

q: Civilian contractors on this project are paid by ______ hour, so overtime gets expensive fast.
e: 'By the + unit' shows how something is measured or paid: by the hour, by the day, by the gallon.

q: The storm hit the base on Tuesday night, and the power didn't come back on until ______ next day.
e: Seen from the past, we say 'the next day' (= the following day); 'next day' alone is not standard here.

q: ______ discipline is important in any unit, but ______ discipline that Sergeant Cole demanded was extreme.
e: Abstract nouns used in general take no article (Discipline is important); a clause that makes them specific needs 'the' (the discipline that he demanded).

q: It was ______ long flight from Kuwait that most of us slept the whole way.
e: 'Such a + adjective + singular noun + that': such a long flight that ... ('So' goes with an adjective alone: so long that ...).

q: Most of ______ soldiers in my company have deployed at least twice, but I'm still waiting for my first time.
e: 'Most of' must be followed by a determiner (the, my, these): most of the soldiers. Without 'of', say 'most soldiers'.

q: The new barracks are modern, but ______ soldiers want to live there because they're so far from the gym and the dining facility.
e: 'Few' (without 'a') is negative: almost no soldiers. 'Little' is used with uncountable nouns.

q: Don't worry about running out of forms; I still have ______ blank ones in my desk drawer.
e: 'A few' is positive (some, enough) and goes with countable nouns like forms.

q: Quite ______ people showed up for the 5K run on post, even though it was pouring rain.
e: 'Quite a few' means a fairly large number of people. 'Quite few' is not used.

q: I've been to Germany ______ times, so I can show you around Ramstein when you get there.
e: 'A few times' = several times, enough experience to help. 'Few times' would mean almost never, which contradicts the offer.

q: During the night, the sentry has to walk the fence line every ______ hours and report anything unusual.
e: After 'every', use 'few' without 'a': every few hours, every few days.

q: Since ______ of us knew the area, we had to rely completely on the GPS and the map.
e: 'Few of us' = almost none of us, which explains the total reliance on the GPS. 'A few' would be positive.

q: The colonel's speech had ______ effect on the troops; most of them were still angry when it ended.
e: 'Little' (without 'a') is negative: almost no effect. Here 'effect' is uncountable, so 'few' is wrong.

q: Could you speak ______ more slowly? The connection on this line keeps breaking up.
e: 'A little' + comparative means 'slightly': a little more slowly, a little louder.

q: There's still ______ fuel in the generator, so we can keep the lights on for another hour.
e: 'A little' is positive (some, enough) and goes with uncountable nouns like fuel.

q: He made very ______ progress in his first month of language training, but things improved once he got a tutor.
e: 'Very little' + uncountable noun (progress) = almost none. 'Very a little' and 'very less' are not possible; 'progress' is uncountable, so not 'few'.

q: After nine days under the rubble, there is ______ hope of finding more survivors, so the search will end tonight.
e: 'Little hope' = almost no hope, which is why the search will end. 'Hope' is uncountable, so 'few' is wrong.

q: I only know ______ Korean, but it was enough to order food and ask for directions in Seoul.
e: 'Only a little' = a small but useful amount of something uncountable. 'Only little' is not standard.

q: ______ of the four tires was checked for wear before the convoy left the motor pool.
e: 'Each of + plural noun' takes a singular verb. 'Every' cannot be followed by 'of'; 'all' and 'both' need a plural verb.

q: The shuttle bus to the airport leaves ______ twenty minutes, starting at 0500.
e: For regular intervals, use 'every': every twenty minutes, every other day.

q: Almost ______ soldier in the platoon passed the swim qualification on the first try.
e: 'Almost' and 'nearly' can come before 'every' but not before 'each'. 'All' would need a plural noun.

q: Before the desert march, the instructors handed the recruits two canteens ______.
e: 'Each' can come at the end of a clause to mean 'for every one of them': two canteens each. 'Every' cannot be used alone like this.

q: ______ single member of the team has to sign the safety roster before the jump.
e: 'Every single' is used for emphasis; 'each single' is not used, and 'all' and 'both' need a plural noun.

q: Every officer and every NCO in the battalion ______ expected to attend the change-of-command ceremony.
e: Subjects with 'every' (even 'every X and every Y') take a singular verb.

q: Two sentries stood on ______ side of the gate, checking IDs as the cars came through.
e: 'On either side' = on each of the two sides. 'Both' needs a plural noun (both sides), and 'every' is not used for two things.

q: We tried two different radios, but ______ of them could reach the base.
e: For two things, the negative is 'neither of them'. 'None' is used for three or more.

q: I don't like working the night shift, and my roommate doesn't ______.
e: After a negative verb (doesn't), use 'either' to agree: I don't, and he doesn't either.

q: A: I've never been stationed overseas. B: ______ have I. I'm hoping for Japan next year.
e: To agree with a negative statement, use 'Neither + auxiliary + subject': Neither have I. 'So have I' agrees with a positive statement.

q: You can take ______ the 0600 bus or the 0730 bus; both will get you to the range in time.
e: 'Either ... or' presents a choice between two options.

q: ______ the captain nor the first sergeant knew about the schedule change until Friday afternoon.
e: 'Neither ... nor' makes a negative statement about two people or things.

q: Neither the platoon leader nor his soldiers ______ aware that the route had been changed.
e: With 'neither ... nor', the verb agrees with the nearer subject: ... nor his soldiers were.

q: The graduation ceremony will take place ______ the morning of June 6, weather permitting.
e: We say 'in the morning', but 'on the morning of + date' because a specific day is named.

q: Please have the vehicle inspection reports on my desk ______ 1600 at the latest.
e: 'By' = no later than (a deadline). 'Until' describes a situation that continues up to a time.

q: The road to Range 12 will be closed ______ further notice because of the fire danger.
e: 'Until further notice' = the situation continues up to the time you are told otherwise.

q: By the time she retires next May, she will have been in the Army ______ twenty-two years.
e: 'For' + a period of time (twenty-two years); 'since' + a starting point (since 2004).

q: The new commander arrived ______ Christmas Eve, just as half the unit was going on leave.
e: Use 'on' for a specific day: on Christmas Eve, on July 4. 'At Christmas' means the holiday period.

q: The dining facility serves breakfast ______ 0600 to 0800 on weekdays.
e: 'From ... to' gives the start and end times. 'Between' must be followed by 'and', not 'to'.

q: The colonel will be on leave ______ the 3rd and the 17th of August.
e: 'Between ... and' marks a period with two limits. 'From' would need 'to' or 'until'.

q: He was promoted to staff sergeant ______ the age of twenty-four.
e: We say 'at the age of + number' (or simply 'at twenty-four').

q: Your new ID card will be ready ______ two weeks; we'll call you when it comes in.
e: 'In + period' = that much time from now: in two weeks. 'Ago' is for the past; 'by' needs a point in time.

q: ______ the end of the movie, almost everyone in the theater was in tears.
e: 'At the end of + noun' = at the final point of something. 'In the end' (without 'of') means 'finally'.

q: We argued about the route for over an hour, but ______ the end we followed the sergeant's plan.
e: 'In the end' = finally, after a long time or discussion. 'At the end' needs 'of' + noun.

q: My grandfather joined the Navy ______ 1960s, when he was just eighteen years old.
e: Decades take 'in the': in the 1960s, in the nineties.

q: Private Banks fell asleep ______ the safety briefing and was given extra duty for a week.
e: 'During' + noun (during the briefing); 'while' + clause (while the sergeant was talking).

q: The new duty roster has been posted ______ the bulletin board outside the orderly room.
e: Use 'on' for a surface: on the bulletin board, on the wall, on the screen.

q: The recruiting office is ______ the second floor of the old bank building ______ the corner of Elm and Third.
e: Floors take 'on' (on the second floor); in American English a street corner also takes 'on' (on the corner of Elm and Third).

q: They used to live ______ Pine Street, but last year they moved to a house ______ 41 Harbor Road.
e: American English: 'on' + street name (on Pine Street), but 'at' + an exact address with a number (at 41 Harbor Road).

q: We waited ______ line for over an hour to get our flu shots at the clinic.
e: In American English you wait or stand 'in line'.

q: The medic knelt ______ the wounded soldier and checked his breathing.
e: 'Beside' = next to. 'Besides' = in addition to; 'between' and 'among' need two or more people or things.

q: There's a gas station right ______ the road from the main gate, so you can't miss it.
e: 'Across the road/street from' = on the opposite side of the road.

q: The sniper was hiding ______ a pile of rubble ______ the far end of the street.
e: 'Behind' = at the back of; 'at the end of the street' marks a point. 'In the end' means 'finally'.

q: We left the base ______ a taxi, but we came back ______ the shuttle bus.
e: Use 'in' for cars and taxis, 'on' for buses, trains and planes. 'By' is used without an article: by taxi, by bus.

q: Who is the tall officer standing next to you ______ this photo?
e: People and things appear 'in' a photo or picture, not 'on' it.

q: You'll find the wiring diagram ______ page 47 of the technical manual.
e: Use 'on' with page numbers: on page 47.

q: The printer is ______ the corner of the office, and the coffee shop is ______ the corner of Oak and Second.
e: 'In the corner' of a room (inside it), but 'on the corner' of two streets (American English).

q: Fort Drum is located ______ upstate New York, not far from the Canadian border.
e: Use 'in' with states, regions and countries: in upstate New York, in Texas.

q: All personnel must refrain ______ smoking within fifty feet of the fuel point.
e: 'Refrain from + -ing' = not do something.

q: The new training program consists ______ four phases, each lasting three weeks.
e: 'Consist of' = be made up of.

q: Corporal Lee is eligible ______ promotion, but she has to finish the leadership course first.
e: 'Eligible for + noun' (eligible for promotion); 'eligible to + verb' (eligible to vote).

q: Several soldiers objected ______ moved to the older barracks on the far side of post.
e: 'Object to' is followed by a gerund because 'to' is a preposition here: object to being moved.

q: We look forward ______ you at the reunion in San Antonio next summer.
e: 'Look forward to + -ing': 'to' is a preposition, so the verb takes -ing.

q: The new software is familiar ______ most clerks, but the new sergeant isn't familiar ______ it yet.
e: Something is familiar TO a person; a person is familiar WITH something.

q: If you want a transfer, you need to apply ______ the personnel office ______ a new assignment.
e: You apply TO a place or person FOR the thing you want.

q: I'm really grateful ______ my platoon sergeant ______ all the help he gave me during my first year.
e: Grateful TO a person FOR something.

q: There has been a sharp increase ______ the number of applicants for the Special Forces course.
e: 'An increase in' + the thing that grows; 'an increase of' + the amount (an increase of 20 percent).

q: The storm caused serious damage ______ two hangars and several parked helicopters.
e: The noun 'damage' is followed by 'to': damage to the hangars.

q: Private Grant was charged ______ assault after a fight in the parking lot of a bar.
e: Charged WITH a crime (but accused OF a crime).

q: The lieutenant took advantage ______ the darkness to move his platoon closer to the ridge.
e: 'Take advantage of' = use a situation for your benefit.

q: The fire resulted ______ a faulty heater, and it resulted ______ the loss of two vehicles.
e: 'Result from' + the cause; 'result in' + the consequence.

q: She takes great pride ______ her work as a flight medic.
e: 'Take pride in' something (but 'be proud of' something).

q: Her parents never approved ______ her decision to join the Marines, but they came to her graduation anyway.
e: 'Approve of' = think that something is good or acceptable.

q: The new regulations prevent soldiers ______ bringing privately owned weapons onto the installation.
e: 'Prevent someone from + -ing' = stop them from doing it.

q: The contractor's new translator specializes ______ legal and technical documents.
e: 'Specialize in' = concentrate on one area of work.

q: A squad leader is responsible ______ the safety of his soldiers, and he is responsible ______ the platoon sergeant.
e: Responsible FOR a task or the people in your care; responsible TO the person you report to.

q: I'm fed up ______ cleaning up after people who leave their trash in the dayroom.
e: In American English you are 'fed up with' something = annoyed and tired of it.

q: Nobody could account ______ the missing night-vision goggles after the exercise.
e: 'Account for' = explain where something is or why something happened.

q: The new rifle is superior ______ the old model in almost every way.
e: 'Superior' and 'inferior' take 'to', not 'than'.

q: There is a growing demand ______ soldiers who can speak Korean or Japanese.
e: The noun 'demand' takes 'for': a demand for linguists.

q: Many of the families are strongly opposed ______ the plan to close the base hospital.
e: 'Be opposed to' something; 'against' is used without 'opposed': They are against the plan.

q: Do you have access ______ the classified network from your workstation?
e: The noun 'access' takes 'to': access to the network.

q: There is no alternative ______ hard work if you want to pass the ECL with a high score.
e: 'An alternative to' something = another option instead of it.

q: ______ the forecast had promised clear skies, the night jump was canceled because of high winds.
e: Although + full clause shows contrast; despite needs a noun or -ing form, and however / therefore cannot join two clauses this way.

q: Sergeant Ortiz completed the twelve-mile ruck march ______ a badly sprained ankle.
e: In spite of + noun phrase; even though, although and whereas must be followed by a clause (subject + verb).

q: The first platoon reached the objective right on schedule, ______ the second platoon got lost in the woods.
e: Whereas contrasts two different facts or groups; despite / in spite of need a noun, and therefore shows a result.

q: The new radios are lighter and easier to carry; ______, most operators still prefer the old ones.
e: However (after a semicolon, before a comma) links two sentences with a contrast; whereas and although are conjunctions and cannot be used this way.

q: Corporal Diaz had let his security clearance expire; ______, he was denied access to the operations center.
e: Therefore introduces a logical result: the expired clearance caused the denial of access.

q: ______ being the youngest member of the team, Specialist Kim was chosen to lead the briefing.
e: Despite + -ing form (despite being); even though and whereas need a subject and verb, and however does not introduce a phrase.

q: The supply truck arrived three hours late. ______, the cooks managed to serve dinner on time.
e: Nevertheless (= in spite of that) can start a new sentence to show contrast; although and despite cannot stand alone before a comma.

q: ______ she had never driven a Humvee before, Private Hale handled it like an expert during the exercise.
e: Even though + clause expresses a strong contrast; in spite of needs a noun or -ing form.

q: My brother enjoys working at a desk all day, ______ I would much rather be out in the field.
e: Whereas compares two opposite situations: his preference and mine.

q: The exercise went ahead as planned ______ the fact that two of the trucks had broken down.
e: Despite the fact that + clause; in spite needs 'of' (in spite of the fact that), and although is followed directly by a clause.

q: The night navigation course was long and exhausting. It was worth every minute, ______.
e: Though can come at the end of a sentence meaning 'however'; although and even though cannot be used in final position.

q: In spite of ______ the map carefully, the patrol took a wrong turn at the river.
e: After the preposition in spite of, use a gerund (-ing) or a noun, not a clause, an infinitive or a past form.

q: ______ some soldiers like the early PT session, others find it very hard to get up at 0500.
e: While can mean 'whereas', contrasting two groups in the same sentence.

q: The pilot could not see the runway ______ the thick fog, so she diverted to another airfield.
e: Because of + noun gives the reason; despite would show contrast, which makes no sense here, and although / whereas need a clause.

q: Fuel supplies were running dangerously low; ______, the commander cut the exercise short by two days.
e: Consequently (= as a result) links a cause to its result; nevertheless would show contrast.

q: Her test results were excellent. The promotion board, ______, decided to wait another year.
e: However can go in the middle of a sentence, between commas, to show contrast; therefore would wrongly suggest a result.

q: ______ all our efforts, the old generator refused to start, and we spent the night without power.
e: Despite + noun phrase, never 'despite of'; although would need a clause.

q: The airfield is completely fogged in, and ______ all flights have been delayed until further notice.
e: And therefore introduces a result; however would show contrast, and whereas / although would leave the sentence incomplete.

q: ______ the old barracks had shared bathrooms, each room in the new building has its own.
e: Whereas introduces a contrast between two situations: the old barracks and the new building.

q: ______ it rains tomorrow, the change-of-command ceremony will still take place on the parade field.
e: Even if introduces a possible (uncertain) situation; even though is used for facts that are already true.

q: The mission was a success in spite of ______ that we lost radio contact for almost an hour.
e: In spite of the fact that + clause: the preposition needs a noun (the fact) before the that-clause.

q: ______ hard he tried, the mechanic could not get the old engine to turn over.
e: However + adjective / adverb means 'no matter how': however hard he tried.

q: Lieutenant Brooks is an excellent marksman; his land navigation skills, ______, still need some work.
e: On the other hand introduces a contrasting point and can sit between commas; whereas and although are conjunctions.

q: Despite ______ in the Navy for twenty years, my uncle still gets seasick on small boats.
e: Despite + perfect gerund (having served) for an earlier action; despite cannot take a clause or an infinitive.

q: The colonel was satisfied with the plan, ______ she asked for a few minor changes to the timeline.
e: Although + clause adds a contrasting fact; despite and because of need a noun, and therefore shows a result.

q: That was ______ coffee I have ever had in a mess hall, and I have tasted a lot of bad coffee.
e: Bad is irregular: bad - worse - the worst. A superlative is used with 'ever'.

q: The new rifle is only ______ heavier than the old one, so most soldiers barely notice the difference.
e: Slightly / a bit / much can modify a comparative; 'very heavier' and 'more heavier' are wrong.

q: The ______ we leave, the better our chances of beating the traffic at the main gate.
e: The + comparative ..., the + comparative ...: the earlier we leave, the better our chances.

q: Fuel costs for the battalion this year are ______ than they were last year.
e: Far / much / a lot strengthen a comparative: far higher; never 'more higher' or 'very higher'.

q: Because of the snow, the drive back to base took twice ______ the drive out.
e: Twice / three times + as ... as: twice as long as.

q: Captain Reyes is ______ officer in the battalion, but she already commands a company.
e: One-syllable adjectives form the superlative with -est: young - the youngest.

q: The more questions you ask during the course, ______ you will learn.
e: The more ..., the more ...: both parts of the double comparative need 'the' + comparative.

q: Please forward the after-action report ______ possible; the general wants it by noon.
e: As soon as possible uses the pattern as + adverb + as.

q: My brother is three years ______ than I am, but he joined the Army after me.
e: Use older with than; elder is only used before a noun (my elder brother), never with than.

q: Thanks to the new budget, the motor pool has twice ______ vehicles as it had last year.
e: Twice as many + plural countable noun + as; much is for uncountable nouns.

q: The new body armor is far superior ______ the old model in both weight and protection.
e: Superior and inferior take 'to', not 'than': superior to the old model.

q: Camp Ridley is the ______ largest training area in the state, after Fort Kendall.
e: Ordinal number + superlative: the second largest, the third biggest.

q: Staff Sergeant Ruiz is one of the ______ in the whole maintenance company.
e: One of the + superlative + plural noun: one of the best mechanics.

q: The second land navigation test was hard, but the third one was ______ harder.
e: Even strengthens a comparative (even harder); very, more and so are not used before a comparative like this.

q: As the storm moved closer to the coast, the waves grew ______.
e: Comparative + and + comparative shows a gradual change: bigger and bigger.

q: The new boots are ______ comfortable than the old ones, so most of the troops dislike them.
e: Less + adjective + than is the opposite of more ... than; fewer is only used with plural nouns.

q: That was the ______ interesting lecture of the whole course; half the class fell asleep.
e: The least + adjective is the opposite of the most + adjective.

q: Even though she is fifteen years older, my mother still runs faster than ______.
e: After than, repeat the auxiliary that matches the verb: she runs faster than I do.

q: This is the longest deployment our unit has ______ had, and morale is starting to drop.
e: Superlative + present perfect + ever: the longest deployment we have ever had.

q: The new engine is three times ______ than the one it replaced.
e: Three times + comparative + than (or three times as ... as); 'as powerful than' is wrong.

q: The more tired you are, ______ attention you pay to small details.
e: The more ..., the less ...; attention is uncountable, so less, not fewer.

q: Could you speak a little ______? The radio connection is very bad.
e: The comparative of the adverb slowly is more slowly.

q: We will need ______ more volunteers if we want to finish loading the trucks before dark.
e: Many more + plural countable noun (volunteers); much more is for uncountable nouns.

q: The updated procedure is no ______ than the old one; it still takes almost three hours.
e: No + comparative + than means 'not at all more': no faster than the old one.

q: Your score on the reading test was exactly the same ______ mine.
e: The same ... as: the same as mine (not 'the same than' or 'the same like').

q: Hardly ______ when the phone rang again with another request from headquarters.
e: Hardly at the start of a sentence needs inversion with the past perfect: Hardly had I ... when ...

q: No sooner ______ the report than the general asked for a revised version.
e: No sooner + had + subject + past participle ... than ...: inversion is required.

q: Not until every soldier was accounted for ______ the platoon leader allow himself to rest.
e: Not until + time clause at the start causes inversion in the main clause: did + subject + base form (allow).

q: Not until we reached the coast ______ how badly the storm had damaged the town.
e: After 'Not until ...' at the beginning, the main clause takes question word order: did we realize.

q: Only then ______ that the map we had been using was twenty years out of date.
e: Only then at the start of a sentence causes inversion: Only then did we notice ...

q: The sign-up sheet was full by noon. Never before ______ so many volunteers for a weekend detail.
e: Never before at the front requires inversion: had + subject + past participle.

q: Seldom ______ a recruit pass the swim qualification on the first attempt.
e: Seldom at the start causes inversion with does + singular subject + base form (pass).

q: Rarely ______ such a well-organized change-of-command ceremony.
e: Rarely at the start causes inversion: Rarely have I attended ...

q: Little ______ that the inspection team was already waiting in his office.
e: Little (= not at all) at the start requires inversion: Little did he know ...

q: Under no circumstances ______ to leave the compound without your weapon.
e: Under no circumstances is already negative: it takes inversion (are you allowed) and no second 'not'.

q: Only after the medic had checked his vital signs ______ to return to duty.
e: Only after + clause at the start causes inversion in the main clause: was the soldier allowed.

q: Not only ______ late for the inspection, but he had also left his boots unpolished.
e: Not only at the start causes inversion; with be, the verb itself moves before the subject: was he.

q: At no time ______ the classified documents out of her sight during the flight.
e: At no time (= never) at the start causes inversion: did + subject + base form.

q: Only when the all-clear sounded ______ to leave the shelter.
e: Only when + clause causes inversion in the main clause: were we permitted (passive).

q: Only by working through the night ______ to meet the deadline for the inspection.
e: Only by + -ing at the start causes inversion: were we able.

q: In no way ______ responsible for the delay; the trucks broke down on the highway.
e: In no way (negative) at the start causes inversion with be: was the driver.

q: Never in my twenty years of service ______ a unit so well prepared for an inspection.
e: Never at the start causes inversion: have I seen.

q: Nowhere ______ better training facilities than at this academy.
e: Nowhere at the front of a sentence causes inversion: will you find.

q: Hardly ever ______ the colonel raise his voice, so everyone listened when he did.
e: Hardly ever at the start causes inversion; past simple uses did + subject + base form.

q: ______ had the ceasefire been announced than people began celebrating in the streets.
e: No sooner ... than is a fixed pair; hardly goes with when, not than.

q: Only now ______ to understand why my old drill sergeant was so strict with us.
e: Only now at the start causes inversion: am I beginning.

q: Never before ______ such a large exercise been held in the region, so the local residents were curious.
e: Never before + had + subject + been + past participle: inversion in the past perfect passive.

q: Not once ______ during the entire six-month deployment.
e: Not once at the start causes inversion with did + subject + base form.

q: Only in an emergency ______ the red button on the control panel.
e: Only + prepositional phrase at the start causes inversion: should you press.

q: Scarcely ______ the contract when the supplier announced a price increase.
e: Scarcely, like hardly, takes inversion with the past perfect and is followed by when.

q: It was ______ hot day that the training was moved to the early morning.
e: Such + a + adjective + singular noun ... that: such a hot day that.

q: The new instructions were ______ confusing that half the class had to ask for help.
e: So + adjective (no noun) + that: so confusing that; too cannot be followed by a that-clause of result.

q: There were ______ people at the air show that we could not find a parking spot.
e: So many + plural countable noun + that; much is for uncountable nouns, and 'such many' is wrong.

q: We had ______ bad weather during the exercise that two helicopters were grounded.
e: Such + adjective + uncountable noun (weather), with no article; so cannot come before adjective + noun.

q: The generators made ______ noise that nobody in the tents could sleep.
e: So much + uncountable noun (noise) + that; so many is for plural countable nouns.

q: So ______ was the explosion that windows shattered more than a mile away.
e: So + adjective + be + subject (inversion): So powerful was the explosion that ...

q: ______ was the demand for the new tablets that the PX sold out within an hour.
e: Such + be + noun ... that (inversion) means 'the demand was so great that ...'.

q: Sergeant Moreno speaks English ______ fluently that people often think she grew up in Texas.
e: So + adverb + that: so fluently that; very cannot introduce a result clause.

q: There was ______ little time left that we had to skip the final rehearsal.
e: So + little / few / much / many + noun + that: so little time that.

q: We received ______ complaints about the food that the mess hall changed its menu.
e: Such a lot of + noun ... that; so cannot come before 'a lot of'.

q: It was ______ an important mission that the general briefed the team himself.
e: Such + an + adjective + noun; the article is already in the sentence, so only 'such' fits.

q: It was ______ good a plan that the commander approved it without a single change.
e: So + adjective + a + noun (formal style): so good a plan = such a good plan.

q: The fog was ______ thick for the pilots to see the runway lights.
e: Too + adjective + for someone + to-infinitive; so would need a that-clause, and enough comes after the adjective.

q: The equipment was so heavy ______ it took four soldiers to lift it.
e: So + adjective + that introduces the result.

q: Nobody would be ______ foolish as to swim in the river during a flood.
e: So + adjective + as to + infinitive means 'foolish enough to'.

q: Speak into the microphone ______ everyone in the back of the room can hear you.
e: So that + clause expresses purpose; so as and in order need 'to' + infinitive.

q: We had such ______ at the reunion that we decided to stay an extra day.
e: Such + a + adjective + singular noun: such a good time.

q: I have never seen ______ in a barracks room before; there were clothes everywhere.
e: Such + a + singular countable noun: such a mess (never 'so a mess' or 'a such mess').

q: Why are you in ______ a hurry? The bus to the airport doesn't leave until noon.
e: Such + a + noun: in such a hurry.

q: The reading test was ______ easy! I finished it in ten minutes.
e: So + adjective with no noun after it: so easy; such needs a noun.

q: So exhausted ______ after the 36-hour shift that he fell asleep standing up.
e: So + adjective at the start causes inversion with be: So exhausted was the guard that ...

q: They are ______ reliable vehicles that the Army has kept them in service for forty years.
e: Such + adjective + plural noun, with no article: such reliable vehicles.

q: Sergeant Clark has already finished his reports, and so ______ the other squad leaders.
e: So + auxiliary + subject means 'also'; the auxiliary matches the first verb (has finished) and the plural subject: so have.

q: Pack warm clothing, ______ gloves, a wool cap and thermal socks.
e: Such as introduces examples.

q: The damage to the bridge was such ______ it had to be rebuilt from scratch.
e: Be + such + that (formal) means 'so great that'.

q: Does your squad ______ a spare key for the equipment room, or should we ask the supply sergeant?
e: After does/do/did, the main verb stays in the base form: Does your squad have...?

q: ______ is to take the express train.
o: The quickest way to reach the airport
The quickest way the airport to reach
The airport to reach the quickest way
To reach the quickest way the airport
e: A noun phrase with an infinitive: the way + to + verb + object (the quickest way to reach the airport).

q: "Does Corporal Evans ever arrive late for formation?" "No, ______."
o: he never arrives late for formation
he arrives never late for formation
never he arrives late for formation
he arrives late for formation never
e: Adverbs of frequency such as never go before the main verb: he never arrives.

q: "The deadline for leave requests is tomorrow morning." "I know. I ______ turn mine in tonight."
e: Must + base verb expresses strong necessity; ought needs to (ought to) and had needs better (had better).

q: A stethoscope is used for ______ a patient's heartbeat and breathing.
e: After a preposition such as for, use the -ing form: used for listening.

q: The night guard didn't see ______ near the fence, so he wrote "all quiet" in his log.
e: After a negative verb (didn't see), use an any- word; a no- word would make a double negative.

q: Choose the correct sentence: ______
o: Captain Reyes needs to finish the training schedule before Friday morning.
Captain Reyes needs finish to the training schedule before Friday morning.
Captain Reyes needs to finish before Friday morning the training schedule.
Captain Reyes needs to the training schedule finish before Friday morning.
e: Word order: subject + verb + to-infinitive + object, with the time expression at the end.

q: Many cities now have bike-sharing programs. A bike costs only a few dollars to rent, and there are stations all over town where it can be picked up or returned. According to this paragraph, bike sharing is ______.
e: The text mentions a low price and many pick-up points, so bike sharing is both cheap and convenient.

q: The helicopter ascended rapidly after takeoff. It went ______.
e: Ascend = go up; the opposite, descend, means go down.

q: Could you call back later? Sergeant Diaz ______ the generator behind the motor pool right now.
e: Right now = an action in progress: present continuous (is + -ing).

q: Choose the correct sentence: ______
o: The new trailer can carry three tons of gravel.
The new trailer can three tons of gravel carry.
The new trailer three tons of gravel can carry.
The new trailer carry can three tons of gravel.
e: Word order: subject + modal (can) + main verb (carry) + object (three tons of gravel).

q: Which is the grammatically correct sentence? ______
o: Could you show me where to plug in this charger?
Where to plug in this charger could you show me?
Could you show me this charger where to plug in?
Could you where to plug in this charger show me?
e: Question order first (Could you show me), then the embedded part: where to + verb + object.

q: The supply room was out of shampoo, so Private Kim took a bar of ______ instead.
e: A bar of soap; milk comes in a carton or a gallon, toothpaste in a tube, rice in a bag.

q: Private Novak cut his finger on the sharp edge of a metal box. He needs ______.
e: A small cut is covered with a bandage.

q: The rolls at the dining hall are always fresh. They are ______.
e: Fresh bread has just been made; it is not frozen, old or stale.

q: Sergeant Lopez *wasn't able to* finish the report before the deadline.
e: Wasn't able to = couldn't (past ability), not a lack of permission or need.

q: On Monday the convoy left an hour late because the drivers ______ start without signed orders.
e: Past situation (left late): the past of can't is couldn't = were not able to.

q: My cousin is hoping ______ a job at the airport after he finishes flight school.
e: Hope is followed by to + verb: hope to find.

q: Choose the correct sentence: ______
o: The pilots walked slowly to the hangar after the briefing.
The pilots slowly to the hangar walked after the briefing.
The pilots walked to slowly the hangar after the briefing.
After the briefing walked the pilots slowly to the hangar.
e: Normal order: subject + verb + manner (slowly) + place (to the hangar) + time (after the briefing).

q: A holster is used to ______ a pistol at your side so that your hands stay free.
e: A holster is a case worn on the belt or body to carry a pistol.

q: Several barracks were badly damaged by a tornado on Friday. They were hit by ______.
e: A tornado is a violent, spinning windstorm.

q: Let's stop at the commissary on the way home; we've almost run ______ coffee and sugar.
e: Run out of something = use all of it and have none left.

q: The old footbridge, ______ by the spring floods, was closed to traffic until engineers could inspect it.
e: A past participle can replace a passive clause after a noun: the footbridge (which was) weakened by the floods.

q: Private Alvarez ______ for his medical clearance for two weeks, and he still has not received an answer.
e: For + a period that continues up to now takes the present perfect continuous: has been waiting.

q: The new duty schedule may ______ to every unit by Friday, but nothing is confirmed yet.
e: Modal + be + past participle makes the passive: may be sent.

q: There were a few small problems with the equipment, but ______, the training exercise was a success.
e: On the whole = in general, considering everything together.

q: Corporal Haddad *agreed to check* the radios before the exercise began.
o: He said he would check them himself.
He said someone else should check them.
He said he had already checked them.
He said nobody could check them.
e: Agree to do something = say that you will do it.

q: Many people believe they can work well on very little sleep. Studies show, however, that tired soldiers make more mistakes and react more slowly than rested ones. According to this paragraph, ______.
o: lack of sleep can hurt performance
tired soldiers are usually more careful
most people need only a few hours of rest
e: The studies show that tired soldiers make more mistakes and react slowly, so lack of sleep hurts performance.

q: Would you ______ moving your truck? It is blocking the gate.
e: Would you mind + -ing is a polite way to ask someone to do something.

q: ______ is the weight limit for each suitcase on this flight? I don't want to pay extra.
e: Ask about a thing or an amount with What: What is the weight limit?

q: The old warehouse looks ______ a museum than a place for storing crates.
e: More like X than Y = closer in appearance or nature to X than to Y.

q: If you see Captain Nasser in the hallway, ______ him that the briefing starts at nine.
e: A request after an if-clause uses the base form (imperative): tell him.

q: Lieutenant Cho's ______ the marathon in under three hours surprised everyone in the unit.
e: After a possessive (Cho's) a gerund works as a noun: Cho's finishing the marathon.

q: Offices use different kinds of clocks. The 12-hour clock, with a.m. and p.m., is common in daily life. The 24-hour clock avoids confusion by counting the hours from 00 to 23. From this paragraph, we learn that the 24-hour clock ______.
o: does not need a.m. or p.m.
has fewer hours than the other
is hard to read at night
e: Each hour has its own number from 00 to 23, so a.m. and p.m. are not needed.

q: The new pilots were asked to answer the questions ______, with no time to prepare.
e: An adverb (-ly) describes how they answered: spontaneously.

q: "Have you ever ridden in a helicopter?" "No, ______."
o: I have never ridden in one
I have ridden never in one
never I have ridden in one
I have ridden in one never
e: Adverbs of frequency like "never" go after the auxiliary (have) and before the main verb.

q: I visit my grandmother every Sunday, and my cousin Malik ______ on Wednesdays.
e: Third person singular needs -s (visits), and after a verb we use the object pronoun "her".

q: Choose the correct sentence: ______
o: Don't leave your rifle in the vehicle overnight.
In the vehicle overnight don't leave your rifle.
Don't your rifle leave in the vehicle overnight.
Your rifle don't leave in the vehicle overnight.
e: Negative command: Don't + verb + object + place + time.

q: The medic grabbed a ______ of scissors and carefully cut open the soldier's sleeve.
e: Things with two matching parts (scissors, pants, glasses) take "a pair of".

q: Soldiers who need prescription medicine usually pick it up ______.
e: A pharmacy is the place that prepares and gives out medicine.

q: Private Okafor asked the driver, "How far is the airport from here?" He wanted to know the ______.
e: "How far...?" asks about distance.

q: Sergeant Kim *was unable to* attend the morning briefing yesterday.
e: Was unable to = was not able to = couldn't.

q: Everyone must ______ the safety video before using the new firing range.
e: After a modal verb (must, should, can) use the base form: must watch.

q: The company's new delivery van ______ from the parking lot on Friday night.
e: Passive past (was + past participle): someone stole the van; the van did not steal.

q: ______ in front of the fire station is not permitted at any time.
e: A gerund (verb + -ing) can be the subject of a sentence: Parking is not permitted.

q: Energy exists in many forms. Sunlight, the heat from a stove, and the movement of a truck are all examples of energy. According to this paragraph, ______.
o: energy can take more than one form
sunlight and stove heat are exactly alike
energy comes only from the sun
trucks need light in order to move
e: The text gives three different examples, so energy has several forms.

q: Lieutenant Moore ordered the new recruits to mop the hallway. In other words, he said ______.
e: Order someone to do something = tell them they must do it.

q: Traffic on the highway this morning was about the same as on any other Monday. The traffic was ______.
e: "The same as on any other day" = normal, as usual.

q: Loose wires and wet floors are common hazards in a repair shop. In this sentence, "hazards" means ______.
e: Hazards = dangers, things that can hurt people.

q: The pilot was grounded for a month because he had violated several ______.
e: Violate = break; you violate rules, laws or regulations.

q: I'll send you my flight details as soon as the travel office ______ my orders.
e: After "as soon as" (when, before, until) use the present tense for a future action.

q: Your car might overheat on the trip if you ______ check the coolant first.
e: First conditional: if + present simple (don't check), may/might/will in the other clause.

q: ______ a tent in strong wind takes more skill than most beginners expect.
e: An infinitive (to + verb) can be the subject of a sentence: To pitch a tent takes skill.

q: There were a few delays at the start, but ______, the training exercise was a success.
e: Overall = considering everything; it can stand alone, followed by a comma.

q: The commander is ______ this afternoon, but she can meet with you first thing tomorrow.
